speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he could give the house something of a summary of the representations being made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the Minister of Scientific Research of France on the subject of the sale of uranium. It reads as follows:
Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce, Hon. Robert Winters, and French Minister of Scientific Research, Mr. Alain Peyrefitte, had an exchange of views of a general nature today on various aspects of technical co-operation between their two countries. In minister's opinion, their conversation should be seen in the context of growing co-operation between France and Canada, which is reflected in frequent ministerial contacts between the two countries. The conversation enabled the two ministers to review the main question connected with a possible sale of Canadian uranium for use in the development of the French nuclear power program. The ministers had the opportunity during their conversation to clarify the positions of their


Inquiries of the Ministry respective governments. The questions involved will be the subject of further discussion at a later date.

channel of the existing station at Barrie from 3 to 5; (c) authority to change the channel of the existing satellite station at Haliburton from 5 to 4 and to relocate antenna site. While there was nothing secret-

That was on January 10, 1966. I might point out that one of the difficulties I am faced with is that I am not very accustomed to reading aloud, as hon. members know. Usually I am a little more confident about most things than I am about my technical knowledge.
It should have been memorized.

There was nothing secret about these applications. It is not customary

for publicity to be given to applications received in the department prior to their technical examination because of the frequency with which delays, changes or even completely new engineering studies are necessary at this stage. Normally the information regarding applications becomes public when they are transmitted to the Board of Broadcast Governors. Applications cannot be dealt with by the government until they have been considered by the Board of Broadcast Governors.
Perhaps I could say a word about the matter of the C.T.V. network which was also raised. Might I point out that it is not in any way the concern of the Minister of Transport. These applications go direct to the Board of Broadcast Governors. I do not feel I should say anything further about it.

I should like to ask the
minister a question that I had in mind a moment ago. I agree with him that when he is making a technical statement no dog should bark. However, I should like to ask him this. The next Board of Broadcast Governors hearing will be on April 26. The last date for the filing of applications for that hearing was January 11. venture in a position that would not give others a chance to compete.

It would have been easier for someone with a better memory than mine to have replied to the hon. gentleman's question if he had confined himself to the question. If I remember his question correctly, it was to this effect: Would the minister ask the Board of Broadcast Governors to postpone the hearing?
The right hon. gentleman's government, of course, piloted the legislation through the house, which established the Board of Broadcast Governors. He is a distinguished lawyer and I should have thought that he would have known that the minister who answers for the B.B.G. is the Secretary of State and not the Minister of Transport. I would be the last person in the world to seek to usurp the powers, prerogatives or rights of any other minister. I think it would be a tremendous inconvenience to many other applicants, who probably are to be heard by the
B.	B.G., for the hearings to be postponed merely because Mr. Snelgrove's is the only application respecting channel 3.

I have sufficient confidence in the impartiality of the gentleman appointed on the recommendation of the right hon. gentleman to be the head of the B.B.G. to feel sure that merely because there is only one application in respect of this matter it will not automatically be granted. With respect to the right hon. gentleman's other question, I asked him whether he was referring to something recommended by the
C.	B.C. or by the B.B.G. I do not know which he means. Whichever body it was recommended by, obviously it is not something that would be within my administrative responsi-

bilities, for which I am now answering as Minister of Transport. My job is to take the responsibility for the technical assessment of applications by my department and, if those applications are technically correct, to send them on the Board of Broadcast Governors and in doing so not to seek to prejudice the board in any way. That is the way I shall seek to do my duty.

I have just one reference. I know that other hon. members want to speak and I shall be short. I was very glad to hear the dissertation on the law. I am not going to express any disagreement with the minister. May I ask first: Has the minister passed this technical information to the Board of Broadcast Governors yet?

I will repeat again, sir, what I said. The applications have not yet been transmitted to the Board of Broadcast Governors. The technical review is well advanced but has not yet been completed. When this review has been completed, and it would not be possible until then to do anything about it, a decision will be required whether they should be forwarded to the Board of Broadcast Governors. There are three applications.
There is only one in this particular situation and that is the one we are talking about.

The three are interlocking.
I would venture the opinion that the Board of Broadcast Governors would certainly not permit channel 3 to be moved from Barrie and nothing else put in its place. If that were permitted I would think that would be a great injustice.

May I ask a question following something that was said earlier? Did I understand the minister to say that if he expressed a view to the Board of Broadcast Governors along the line that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition asked him to do, namely, to postpone consideration of this application, it would be improper? Is that what I understood him to say?

It seems to me that each of us in life should accept and take those responsibilities that are entrusted to him and not seek to usurp the responsibilities of others.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This parliament saw fit to give to the Minister of Transport the responsibility for the technical evaluation of these applications.


Supply-Transport
It also saw fit to give to the Board of Broadcast Governors the opportunity to hold hearings and decide what recommendations it should make. It does seem to me that it would not be proper, particularly for a minister who is not even answerable in parliament for the Board of Broadcast Governors, to seek in any way to direct or influence their disposition of the matter once it is properly before them. Nor do I think it would be fair to applicants to do so.
It is not before them yet.

Moreover, there have been cases without number since the board was established when they have had only one application before them and it is on the public record that they postponed their consideration of the situation because someone else intervened and asked for a postponement. That is a matter for the board. It is not a matter for the Minister of Transport and I do not think it would be proper for the Minister of Transport to do things which are not his responsibility when parliament has expressly made them the responsibility of a board.
No matter what the injustice?

I was not here yesterday when the minister spoke but I read his speech with interest. I was very much struck by his somewhat self-righteous homily about a person's duty, particularly since in the speech I read he took it upon himself in ringing terms to urge that a transfer from Barrie to Toronto was a good thing, that we ought to protect the Canadian interest in this additional channel, that there is a large population in metropolitan Toronto which is entitled to another channel, and so on. If the minister is going to take one position at one point, surely he ought to take the same position at another. I suggest it is much less reprehensible for him and his colleagues to make a simple representation to the board that in view of the fact they have only one application they should postpone consideration of it until other people have had a chance to make representations than for him to make the kind of speech he made yesterday about what is necessary for Canada and Toronto.

I simply cannot let the misrepresentation of the hon. gentleman, which I am sure is accidental-he probably read my speech hurriedly-go on record unanswered. I did not advocate the transfer of this

channel from Barrie to Toronto at all yesterday. All I said was that I had been told by people who I understood to be technically competent that this was the only channel now left in the existing spectrum which could be available to metropolitan Toronto having regard to the channels already occupied there and having regard to those which are protected under the bilateral agreement with the United States. I also felt that if that channel could be made available to metropolitan Toronto before it was lost it would be a wise thing for Canadians to take advantage of it. That is all I said. In saying that I was not attempting to make any suggestion as to who should occupy that channel.

Mr. Chairman, I will not be dealing today with the matter discussed for some time now, but I appreciate the disappointment of my colleagues of the N.D.P. who would have liked to discuss this very matter.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, since the minister has answered a question, I suggest I might be given an opportunity to ask a supplementary question before we go on. I am not trying to steal the floor from the hon. member for Lapointe.
I agree that if someone wishes to ask a question at this point he should be allowed to do so. I am in full accord with that, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Will the hon.
member for Lapointe please resume his seat.
[Translation1
I would ask the hon. member for Lapointe to resume his seat.
If the hon. member for Lapointe would kindly relinquish the floor now to allow another hon. member to put a question, the Chair will gladly accede to his wishes.
Agreed.

I am grateful for the minister's answer though I will have some comment to make on its technical inadequacies as the debate goes along. His opening statement interested me. I am sure all of us here want to see the maximum use made of the television channels available to Canadians. I wonder whether the minister is aware of the study now being carried on by his own department having to do with new developments and technical advances in television


broadcasting as they affect the location of channels all over Canada. These developments will probably result in several new channels becoming available to Canadians.
I should also like to say that the Board of Broadcast Governors themselves, those responsible for the Fowler report and other officials have recommended that there be no tinkering with any television channels in Canada at all until a complete reallocation can be made. I have a further question for the minister. Did the advice given him concerning the possibility of a new station at Buffalo come from people within his department or from people in the television field outside it?

So far as the first question is concerned, the main function of the telecommunications branch of my department in the field of radio and television broadcasting is, of course, to study the possibility of improvement. This is going on all the time.
I was referring to a specific study.

It is not really a specific study. It is a general study of the whole area. Up to now it has not been the case that applications, except for alternate services -there is already alternate service in Toronto so this case would not fit into that group; otherwise the Board of Broadcast Governors would have very little to do-
Here we go.
Applications have been coming forward steadily. This is a matter, after all, for general consideration. I am here discussing my responsibilities as Minister of Transport.
Has it ever been suggested that if this present move is carried out as now contemplated Ontario will permanently lose more than one television channel?

I would feel that this is an argument which people far more competent than I will ever be in this field may make before the Board of Broadcast Governors which is supposed to protect the interests of Canada in this field.

I am sure the minister does not expect us to let his statement go by without further discussion in view of the nebulous nature of the comment he made in response to the representations addressed to him yesterday. It seems to me that the Leader of the Official Opposition has drawn
Supply-Transport
attention to the essential point which was raised yesterday and to which no reasonable answer has yet been given. Instead we have been offered the specious, roundabout observations which the hon. gentleman is so capable of making.
He still has not addressed himself to the real crux of this matter. We want an answer and we intend to get one from him no matter how difficult it may be. The fact still remains that the procedure adopted by these people is in effect a back door, behind the scenes method of opening up another channel in Toronto and of doubling or quadrupling their investment.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This has been done without any public knowledge. Indeed, as reported yesterday, the application was filed and then the period for making similar applications was closed so that what in fact is happening is that a hearing is to be held in April, the effect of which will be to open up a new lucrative plum, a melon or a "smellon" or whatever it may be called in Toronto, without other interested people having an opportunity to compete and to make representations, people who should be given this opportunity.
The minister stands here today and says he will take no responsibility whatever. He will do nothing to get around this sort of backroom deal and the government will do nothing to see that other interested parties have a right to compete. The minister is so suddenly the very paragon of virtue that he cannot bear to make a suggestion on his own behalf.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, we can make a suggestion on behalf of parliament. So far as I am concerned I do not like the looks of the deal, and I think the government has some responsibility to draw to the attention of the B.B.G. the view of members of this house that they do not want this kind of backroom dealing in the granting of television franchises.
We have not received any indication from the minister of what the government is prepared to do to protect the rights of the viewers. I mentioned yesterday that there are a very large number of Canadians who happen to enjoy looking at certain channels. I am not here as a defender or apologist for the United States channels. They are perfectly able to look after themselves. But why is the minister not prepared to take any action on behalf of the public in this matter? Why is he writing off the million or million and a half Canadians who have built up a long-term


Supply-Transport
viewing pattern? Why does he cavalierly dismiss the rights of these people and say that he as a minister of the Crown is not prepared to make any representations so that this particular interest can be represented? I think it is almost reprehensible that this type of thing could come about and then have the minister sit idly by taking no responsibility and saying he cannot act at all.

Mr. Chairman, I am very grateful to the hon. gentleman, who if he is not always fair is practically always clear, for suggesting that something is the crux of the matter. I will not repeat his adjectives because they are his and he can keep them, but he said that the crux of the matter was this deal. There has been no deal of any description.
These people, exercising their rights as citizens, have made an application to a government department and they are entitled to be treated in exactly the same way as any other applicants would be. The fact that they have made this application does not make channel 3 available for Toronto. All they have done is to apply to the B.B.G. or to seek to apply and they have not even got their application to transfer the channel to Toronto over the first hurdle. The board can perfectly well refuse to recommend that and that will be the end of it. The board can say: We will not transfer it unless it is open for competition.
As I understand it, the members of the board are perfectly free to do that. They are the only people who can do it because this parliament decided that these things should be done by an impartial board, not by the government. If the government sought to do any of these things, the attacks of hon. gentlemen would be twice what they are now.
else in this chamber knows, what the B.B.G. will do when the matter comes before it. I do not know and in order that I will not be accused of any more secrecy I think I should tell the committee I had a letter recently from Mr. Cran of CFRB which I would be very glad to put on the record except that I am not very good at reading, as I have demonstrated. It is a letter saying that he feels that if this channel is to be opened for Toronto it should be open for competition.
I have also had a telegram from another defeated candidate, not a Liberal this time, Mr. Joel Aldred, wanting to know how he could apply. I think he should know without my telling him because he got a licence once in Toronto. Then he had a falling out with someone else and he is now out of the business. I did not take his telegram very seriously although I did reply and say there had been no change in procedure.
There is absolutely nothing about this situation that is not perfectly normal and that has not happened on several occasions since the present Broadcasting Act came into effect. There is nothing whatever the government can do about the transfer of this channel, nothing whatever about who shall have the licence should it be transferred unless there is a recommendation from the B.B.G. after a public hearing, and if the board behaves as it has in the past I am perfectly confident it will hear every interested party before a decision is made.

I know this does not fall within the immediate ambit of the minister's authority, but will the White Paper on Broadcasting be brought down, or however you get a white paper from where it originates to the public, before this hearing takes place?
It should not be forgotten that the people who now occupy this channel have the licence for it. No one else could have applied for this channel so long as they just sat quietly in Barrie and did nothing. Therefore it is by no means certain, merely because these people have made an application in a perfectly ordinary way, that the B.B.G. will see fit even to listen to the suggestion that it be moved to Toronto, and it certainly does not follow, if the board should decide it could be moved to Toronto, that the present licensee would be allowed to have the licence without any kind of competition.
But here I enter into a field of speculation because I do not know, and I hope nobody
I could not say because we do not even know when this hearing will take place.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee listened with interest and appreciation yesterday to the presentation of the hon. member for Danforth as he reviewed some of the circumstances in connection with this matter. I do not propose to go into a great deal of detail but there are a few things that become apparent as the discussion continues. The first is that the minister has elevated himself to a high pedestal of nonpartisan consideration in this matter. Some might be impressed by that but such a transition on his part causes one to doubt that it is



as complete as his capacity for words would indicate it is.
One has to look over this situation and see who comprise this group, how they operate and what has been done within the last year or year and a half in this connection. The minister's explanation does not meet the situation in any way. It is a transparent and, if you will, diaphanous cover-up for a condition of affairs that is such that it surprises me he tries to justify it at all.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
None of this would have seen the light of day if somebody had not found out about the secret plans and manipulations that had their birth last September, I think. Reference will be made to that later. The manner in which this thing has been presented has about it an odoriferous aroma. What is behind all this? If the minister had said, having listened to the argument-I know how impressed he was because he showed it by his appearance-"I feel this matter should not receive early attention", that might have been a different story. In respect of the Board of Broadcast Governors, which exists in name but not in personnel because there are vacancies on the board, when is it to have a full complement of members? This question has been asked but no answer has been forthcoming. This whole thing is surrounded by mystery and, as the minister explains things, by subterfuge. He says: After all, what have I got to do with this? I am the minister and my responsibilities do not in any way encompass the possession of a nose that would smell.
I would be glad to leave that to the right hon. gentleman.

Mr. Chairman, I am telling you that this thing is so smelly it requires no olfactory excellence in order to understand it. It has got all the appearances of a plan to make millions under cover of secrecy and concealment. We have channel 3 and it is vacant.
It is not vacant; there is a licence involved.

The minister is afraid the United States may pick it up. When he wrapped himself in the garments of Canadianism I was impressed, greatly impressed. We do not dare allow the United States to get that channel but there is only one Canadian outfit that is going to be allowed to get it. They have got what the
Supply-Transport
minister describes as the technical qualifications. Even if they have not that they certainly have the political ones.
I asked the minister whether he would give consideration to bringing the circumstances in connection with this matter to the attention of the Board of Broadcast Governors. He is completely right as to his legal powers, and I do not argue with that, but there is something more involved than the exercise of legal powers in connection with this matter.
Perhaps illegal powers?

I will deal with that. It is surprising that the minister did not state:	I
am beginning to get suspicious myself. On the contrary, he is not suspicious. This is a proposition he says, that is aboveboard and we are looking at it from a technical angle. I asked him two questions in this regard and his answer was: I cannot do those things.
If there is only one application before the Board of Broadcast Governors it is perhaps understandable that the board might hold that this matter should not be proceeded with at this time, but what about the rights of others? I am going to review briefly something of the record in this connection. I have in mind what was said by Mr. Royce Frith, a prominent and outstanding-
Grit.
He is a prominent and outstanding man of affairs. He applied for a station licence in Windsor, Ontario, and after he received his licence he said that-
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the right hon. gentleman would give the date of the application and the date of the recommendation by the B.B.G.?
I have not got the dates but, of course, the minister is able to look them up.
I am sure the right hon. gentleman does not want in any way to be unfair.
No.

My recollection is, and I think this is quite correct, that the application was made when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister and the recommendation was also made when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister.

Mr. Chairman, that is exactly right. When we were in oflice there were no politics involved. I thank the hon. gentleman for giving testimony to that effect.


Supply-Transport
I must say that that is the most admirable statement he has made this afternoon.
What the hon. gentleman is saying-
We now hear from the president of the truth squad.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman, a while ago members on that side were saying it was too noisy in the house and they wanted silence.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to rise on a point of order. I wonder whether we could arrange to have this show televised?

Let me say this, Mr. Chairman, that if the Canadian people could see what this government is doing in respect of this television channel it would be a good thing to have the proceedings televised.
After Mr. Frith, this outstanding Liberal, received his licence he said:	"This is a
rare and exciting opportunity for Canadi-anism in the broadcasting media", but a year later he disposed of that station to the Stirling interests.
Who are some of these people who are interested? There is Mr. Snelgrove. In the month of September last he made the announcement that he was going to Ottawa to look after broadcasting for the Liberal party to see that it got a fair deal from the C.B.C. He came and was here throughout the campaign, and it was not very long after that that a most interesting thing took place. On behalf of one of the rival parties in the campaign Ken Soble sent out a letter, which I am not going to go into at the moment, in respect of what was called "Fedmin"-federal minister. This was a wonderful organization and its suggestions for the guidance of radio and television stations were these:
We are thinking in terms of 50 or 60 second excerpts from campaign speeches as they are being delivered from the platform...
The executive assistants will help in pinpointing the part of the address to be sent back. If there is no one travelling with minister, perhaps someone on the scene can select the most newsworthy bit to be sent back.
Then it goes on to state:
Note to News Editors: Assuming that most of these clips are of legitimate news interest, the idea is to expose the minister to his constituents while he's out of the city or province on extended campaigning commitments.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Introductions to the clips should, if possible, point this out: that the Minister has been spending the last few days in such-and-such an area,

and today from the Prairies had this to report to the electors or people of (name of Minister's riding) :-
Well, this was very good; this was wonderful. This was not part of the propaganda financed by the Liberal party; this was a public service. Then it says:
Following are the stations participating, the ministers they are serving, and the executive assistants attached to those ministers:
CJON-TV (St. John's, Newfoundland) for Transport Minister J. W. Pickersgill. See Alistair Fraser or Eric Facey.
CJCB-TV (Sydney, Nova Scotia) for Labour Minister Allan J. MacEachen. See Pat Lavelle.
CJCH-TV (Halifax, Nova Scotia) also for Labour Minister MacEachen.
CFCF-TV (Montreal, Quebec) serving two ministers, Industry Minister C. M. "Bud" Drury. Executive Assistant is Fred Wanklyn. Also President of the Privy Council Guy Favreau. Executive Assistant is Andre Ouellette.
Then it covers Toronto, Hamilton and the Niagara peninsula. It has them all. Then it says:
Finance Minister Walter Gordon (Toronto Davenport) ; Executive Assistant is Alan Donnelly.
Trade and Commerce Minister Mitchell Sharp (Toronto Eglinton); Executive Assistant is Mike McCabe.
Defence Minister Paul T. Hellyer (Toronto Trinity); Special Assistant is Bill Lee.
It then refers to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Solicitor General, and so on. Then it says:
CKLW-TV (Windsor, Ontario) serves Hon. Paul Martin, Minister of External Affairs.
The former minister of trade and commerce came in for extra attention. He had CJAY-TV, Winnipeg, CKCK-TV, Regina and CJQC-TV, Saskatoon. It says:
For our purposes these three stations will be serving Trade and Commerce Minister Mitchell Sharp.
Oh, oh.
What manner of stuff if this? They took the present minister-
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the right hon. gentleman whether somebody was mentioned for the Quebec City television station?
I do not think they got even an honourable mention.
Oh, oh.

It ends up by saying: "All news clips to be shipped to"

and so on-"Pallette Productions".
The name to be used was "Fedmin". When this information got out Mr. Soble said, "Well, if some Conservatives or members of

the N.D.P. would like to be included they can be". I do not know how they could come under this "Fedmin", but as far as I am concerned, I am fed up.
Hear, hear.

Let us go on from there and see what happened thereafter. Mr. Snelgrove did his job. He saw this channel 3 and he made an application. It is the only one that has been made and I believe the date for the closing of applications was January 11. I asked the minister what he was going to do about this and the answer was, "Well, I cannot do anything about it".
I am becoming very concerned, sir, at the degree to which various groups are commencing to control television and radio across this nation. I shall give particulars of this after I receive some answers from the minister. I am going to go into some detail in this regard either today or later and I shall set out something of what is happening when men politically activated and active politically get control of the means of communication within this nation.
What is going to happen in this regard? Are they going to be considerate of those with whom they disagree? Sir, as far as this proposition is concerned I would have thought that the Prime Minister would have risen and said, "This thing cannot go on".
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He doesn't know.

This is an amazing
proposition.
Nobody told him.
They told him in an aeroplane.

Mr. Chairman, surely the minister does not want this house to accept the explanation, "Well, I really do not know anything about this. The very suggestion that there might be anything wrong in it shocks me". I say to the minister, what are you going to do about it? If we cannot get some action from you, we shall have to ask the Prime Minister. This thing is wrong; this thing is improper; this thing cannot be justified. It has all the appearances of a pork-barrel. The minister smiles and sweeps that suggestion aside. It is wrong. We must have an explanation of it.
Imagine what happens, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Snelgrove has this station in the Barrie area; he uses that to get into Toronto and get this channel 3. I do not know the value of his
Supply-Transport
station but I have been told it would not be over $2-2 million as it is today. The minute that he gets this other channel it becomes worth $6 million or $7 million. There is something wrong with a proposition like that. We have the background in the election campaign. No one complains when a public man takes part in public life, but when he comes here, stays here and then the application is made-well, I am not going to say more, Mr. Chairman. We shall have more to say later. But I do say to the minister: Think this over; do not try to pretend that it can be brushed aside, because it cannot.
This thing has about it an atmosphere that is a denial of every principle for which democracy stands. This House of Commons may not have any authority in this connection but this house can speak, and I believe that on the minister's side of the house there are many members who have looked at this and said, "What is this?" For after all, Mr. Chairman, regard for the proprieties is not the monopoly of any party.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This thing cannot be justified. All the minister does is to rise and, excellent parliamentarian that he is, brush the matter aside. He says he has no authority, that he really cannot do anything. He must know in his own heart that this is not the kind of thing that will strengthen democracy. I wish, as someone has said, that these proceedings could be broadcast. I wish the Canadian people could sit before their television screens in judgment on the attitude of the government on a matter such as this. I should like the people to have that opportunity. I still hope, Mr. Chairman, that the government will finally determine that this means of making a fortune by under the table arrangements-I am not going to call it by its proper name-cannot be accepted.

Mr. Chairman, I, like
every other hon. member, I suppose, have been entertained by the parliamentary display we have just witnessed. I am quite sure the hon. member for Danforth might just as well go out in the lobby because he is out of the newspapers for the day.
I rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I feel it is quite clear that none of us on this side of the house is the least bit interested in headlines. We are here to protect the public.

The right hon. gentleman put himself on a pedestal, which he builds


Supply-Transport
with greater skill and greater ease than I would ever hope to be able to do. When he rises on a pedestal and says, I am surprised that the Prime Minister did not say this nefarious thing should not go on, I begin to wonder. After all, he was the minister primarily responsible for the present Broadcasting Act which laid down these procedures.
The right hon. gentleman expressed great concern about the concentration of these vast, influential means of communication in a few hands, and I must say that I agree with much of what he says about that. However, did he take that same view when the publisher of the Toronto Telegram was applying for a licence along with Mr. Joel Aldred-a couple of distinguished Liberals, of course-both of whom subsequently became Tory candidates? Did he at that time say this should not be allowed?
Others had channels.

Nobody knows whether anything will happen in connection with this application until it gets before the board that was set up by this parliament at the instance of the right hon. gentleman. Does the right hon. gentleman say that I, as Minister of Transport, should have denied to Mr. Snel-grove the right which any other person would have had to make this application, a right that Mr. Cran of CFRB will have to make an application or any technical case that he wants to make, a right which even Joel Aldred, if we are to take him seriously, will have to make a second bid?
I have said before and I say again that this application which was made on January 9 could not have been very secret or we would not be having this debate now. Under the law which the right hon. gentleman himself has the primary responsibility for putting on the statute books, nothing can be done about moving this channel without a public hearing by the Board of Broadcast Governors. The right hon. gentleman must know this well, as one of the authors of the law. We can only draw one conclusion, therefore, about the performance he put on this afternoon, because this is the law.
I am informed that neither when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister nor since has it been the practice of the Department of Transport to do anything about these applications except to process them and send them, if they are technically feasible, to the Board of Broadcast Governors. The first time I was asked a question about whether or not there

was an application I made inquiries of my department. I found out it had been received and I said, has it been the custom to make these things public when they are received? They said no, it had not been the custom. I said, is there any reason why we should not and they said they did not see any reason.
I told the person who asked me, who happened to be a correspondent for the Toronto Telegram, that there was such an application and that it had been received for technical assessment. Was that secret? Was there anything unusual about that? The plain fact is that the right hon. gentleman is simply trying to suggest that because certain people happen to be supporters of this government, which many millions of people in this country are, they should be denied the right that other people would have to make an application for what is nothing but a hunting licence. The right hon. gentleman could find a secret in a Coca-Cola advertisement. I have never known anyone else with the capacity he has. No matter how open, how blatantly obvious a thing is, in his mind there is always something hidden. One really wonders, but considering the relationships he has had with his colleagues I can understand why he has these suspicions.
Unless the right hon. gentleman thinks that these would-be applicants, because that is all they are yet, have a very good case which is going to be very persuasive, he should not be worried about having the board hear the case in public. There will be bound to be representations from powerful interests like the owners of CFRB, who are not without influence although apparently they did not have as much as they had hoped to have when they were competing with Mr. Bassett. Of course, the right hon. gentleman cannot be unaware of the fact that the same kind of insinuation was made about Mr. Bassett when the Leader of the Opposition was prime minister as he is trying to make now. At least no attempt was made to pre-judge that case as the right hon. gentleman now seems to be trying to do in this instance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Greenwood.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I shall substantially reduce the entertainment level of this debate in comparison with what we have heard from the last two speakers. However, my constituents are very much


Supply-Transport
concerned about this matter and I want to say a word or two about it. I listened with great interest to the reply the Minister of Transport made to the questions asked by my colleague, the hon. member for Danforth. I must say I thought the Shakespearean expression seemed to be apt, "Methinks he doth protest too much".
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The minister in his reply said, in tones almost too pious to be credible, that it would be wrong and improper for him to take over the jurisdiction of the B.B.G. or even to make representations to that body about the merits of the application that came before him. He may well be right about that. But does he not think it would be within the scope of his duty, as a member of the government and as minister in charge of this matter, to speak for the public when it is known to him that a single applicant is seeking a very valuable channel and property and that the hearing of the matter is coming up shortly? Would he not think it within the purview of his duty to tell the public of this so that any possible competitors would know about it, or even ask the B.B.G. to make sure that this matter is not passed over or dealt with on a single application?
The minister talks about the courts. A court is set up by parliament and even courts are entitled to have all interested parties come before them. How is the public to be represented if the minister sits mute and says nothing or says that he has only a technical interest in this matter?
If the minister is not interested in this matter, then who is? Are members of parliament to find out about this by chance, by reading some column in a newspaper which says that a matter of this importance is coming before the B.B.G.? Must we take the responsibility-we are ready and willing to do so but do not have the facilities, of course-of saying that we will go to the B.B.G. and represent the public who are concerned in this matter? I suggest the minister should concede that he has a much greater responsibility. His reply to the house has been an evasion of that responsibility.
The minister is very convincing when he says that he must not make representations. He is very convincing when he says that the B.B.G. and my right hon. friend's government brought in these regulations. But he is less convincing to me, and I think also to the public, when he says that he is not able to ask the B.B.G to make sure that this matter
is not dealt with in this way. It should not be dealt with in a hole in the corner manner as it may well be if this applicant is the only one when the case is heard in April. On the contrary, there should be an adequate airing of the matter.
The minister says that this matter has been made public. Who made it public? Not the minister or anyone associated with him. It was made public initially through the actions of private members of this house, members of the opposition.
I know the hon. gentleman is always very fair, but I do not think it was made public until I did so in response to a question, the very first question I was asked about the matter.

If I am unfair then I am sorry. I did not intend to be unfair to the minister and would be glad to withdraw that suggestion. But I still say that the minister did not make the matter public till he was asked to by a member of the press. Even today he says that he cannot even ask the B.B.G. to postpone the hearing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a question to the hon. member, whose knowledge of the law I respect. This channel is not now available in Toronto. It is licensed to one licensee in Barrie. If that licensee does not make an application to have it transferred, how can the matter come before the board at all?
Once it comes before the board it is open, is it not, to the board to say: "We will not allow you to transfer but if you want to give up the licence we will open it for competition"? But as I say I do not see how the matter could ever get before the board unless an initiative was taken in the first place by the present licensee. Unless he does something wrong which would justify his licence being taken away from him, under the practice as I understand it nothing whatever could happen about this matter, without an application for transfer.
It might be that circumstances would arise whereby this channel-and this is a serious matter-would be entirely lost to metropolitan Toronto. It also seems to me that we are showing rather little confidence in the fairness and capacity of the board to assess all these things when they hear the matter. I do not think there is any doubt, judging from the feeling which seems to have been expressed in this committee, that the board will not deny a hearing to anybody who wants to


Supply-Transport
make representations and who has any ground for doing so. They never have before. So it seems to me there is no problem at all of the kind the hon. gentleman seems to be fearing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that the minister might be perfectly right-I do not know; I do not profess to be an expert in this field-when he says that until the application for transfer was made nothing could be done. What I am suggesting is that once the application for transfer on a subject of such vast interest to the public was made and despite what he may say about confidence in the B.B.G. at this stage, surely it would be open to the minister, representing the public who are interested in this matter, and indeed right for him to say that this application is a matter of public concern and should be made known so that others who want to make applications or to oppose this one can do so in plenty of time. I know enough about courts, and I do not think the B.B.G. is any exception, to know that if they have a nice, little, quiet, unopposed application before them they like to deal with it in a quiet, summary fashion. This is what we are seeking to prevent.
I suggest to the minister that instead of taking the position that he has no interest in this matter he should say that he will take responsibility now, even at this late stage, for communicating with the B.B.G. and saying to them: "I want you to postpone this matter if necessary so that a full and adequate hearing can be held of all those interested in the matter". Then there can be no smell or odour about this matter, as has been suggested in this committee.

Mr. Chairman, I think I said in my opening statement that when the technical assessment of this application is completed it will be sent to the Board of Broadcast Governors. At that time it will be advertised by the board in the ordinary way. Today is February 10. The hearing is not until April. It does not require a great deal of technical capacity for people to go along to that hearing and object. Since there are many precedents for this kind of intervention it does not seem to me that there is any need for me to depart from what has been the invariable practice up till now of sending the application to the B.B.G. and letting them make it public, which they would have done.

It would have been a very unusual course for me to take if I had gratuitously made this matter public and then the technical assessment, which has not yet been completed, had shown, as it may yet show, that it was not technically feasible to accept the application. In that case there would have been no application to be heard and no occasion for all the discussion and debate which we have had. Notwithstanding the fact that it had not been the practice, the moment I was asked about it I did not attempt to hide anything but gave the information at once.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the statements of the Minister of Transport but I am still astounded by the fact that this matter should even be before the public at the present time. For as long as two years we have heard in this house from whoever happens to be spokesman for the C.B.C., which is a shifting responsibility with this government, that there is absolutely no value in making applications to the Board of Broadcast Governors. A freeze has been on for two years. We were first told that the freeze would remain on until such time as the Fowler Committee reported. When the government received that report we were told that the freeze was to continue because the Prime Minister had decided to set up another committee to determine what the Fowler Committee report said and what the government should do about it.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I, as a member from a constituency in Nova Scotia which is not receiving satisfactory television coverage from the CTV, have written letters and asked questions in the house about what is going to be done with respect to channel 8 which is at present providing a mediocre type of service to the people of Cumberland, Westmorland and Hillsborough counties. I have, for instance, a letter from the Secretary of State which is quite emphatic and straightforward. I would think that if Mr. Snelgrove were other than the gentleman he is, or if he had got in touch with the government as I did on behalf of my constituents, he would h ave received the same type of communication I have here. This is what the Secretary of State said, and I read from her letter dated January 25, 1966: As you are aware, the Board of Broadcast Governors has not proceeded with such applications at the request of the government while the question of providing alternative television service was under policy study.


Mr. Chairman, surely this situation must come four square within this statement.
While, as you have noted, the government now has received the recommendations ol the Fowler committee on this and other matters, it has not as yet had time to reach a decision.
Until such a policy statement has been worked out and announced, the B.B.G. presumably will continue to maintain its current attitude toward applications for the creation or extension of alternate television service. I am afraid that at this stage I am not in a position to give you any firm indication as to when the required policy statement might be made.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State owe to me, to my constituents and to the people in the coverage area of channel 8 in Nova Scotia a very explicit explanation as to what they are trying to pull off here, because there is certainly something that does not meet the meaning of the statement of the Secretary of State as to what is being done about applications. In effect every other television operator in this nation is now being told: Do not bother the B.B.G. until the Prime Minister has decided what he is going to do about the Fowler committee report. At the same time they are saying to Mr. Snelgrove: "Here is a chance for you to make a big bundle of dough so get your application in. If the people don't catch on," as they have, "you will have a lot of money and maybe the Liberal party will too."
In the last parliament the Canadian people got very sick and fed up with this kind of tactic of Liberal bagmen trying to fill the bags for the cause. You can hear them saying that this is a pretty good chance-

speechtext: Order, please.

I think I should clear up the misunderstanding which I think exists. It is quite true that the government has imposed a freeze on alternate service and it might be that the Board of Broadcast Governors would interpret a third application in metropolitan Toronto as coming within that freeze. The understanding I had, as one of the ministers responsible for advising the government at the time the freeze was put on, was that it was a freeze in respect of areas where there was only one emitting service and where there might conceivably be two in order to give the Fowler committee time to advise and then to give the government time to consider whether it would be willing to provide the extra capital for the C.B.C. to establish a second station or whether the area would be left open for a private station.
Supply-Transport
The B.B.G. has had many applications which it has considered and granted for extensions of services where alternate services already existed. I would expect that if this matter does get before the B.B.G. it certainly would be argued, because there is an arguable case, that this is in a sense an alternate service. I will not quibble about words, and I will not quibble whether alternate means one of two and not one of three, because normally it would mean an alternate service. In other words, there is already a private station in the CTV network, as well as a C.B.C. station in Toronto.
The situation which the hon. gentleman refers to, which has been before the B.B.G., and been there, I believe since the freeze order, is that there is some question about whether there might be an originating station either at Amherst or Moncton if the freeze were taken off. However, if a stronger satellite were established this would be likely to preclude that possibility. Whether or not that is a sound position to take I do not know but that, as I understand it, is the position which was taken. I am trying to deal only with the point itself and not with any of the other observations of the hon. gentleman. I think I have stated the situation.

Mr. Chairman, the only reason I want to take part in this debate on

channel 3, the English station in Toronto, is to remind the minister that, at the present time, Toronto has two channels for English television and none for French television.
At this time, since this is the last vacant channel or the last that will be vacant in future, it might be a good idea for the minister to examine the possibility of reserving a station for French television in Toronto.
In Montreal, where 80 per cent of the population is French Canadian, there are two English and two French television stations. In Toronto, where there are nearly 600,000 French Canadians, there are two English stations and no French station.
I think the minister should consider the possibility of recommending to the B.B.G. the use of this last channel for French television.
To my mind, the Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State should consider this request. In fact, it would only be fair for the
600,000	French Canadians living in the Toronto area and it would close the discussion arising from this application for a third English language television station when there is not a single French language station.
I think my hon. friend the member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) will approve the suggestion I am making. Looking at him brings to mind the remarks he made yesterday about Montreal, saying he was surprised that there was not a more up to date sewer system in a city anxious to show its high degree of civilization in connection with Expo '67.
Mr. Chairman, I must say that I never judged a nation's civilization by its sewer system. The degree of civilization cannot be judged by the perfection of sewer systems, because I would say then that the world's greatest civilizations, either that of the Greeks at the time of Pericles or that of the Romans at the time of-

I am grateful to the hon.
member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) who does not want to miss a single word of what I am saying now and if the translation system is now working, I am very happy for him.
[Mr Gregoire.]
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, a people's, civilization cannot be judged by its sewer system; it would be a very poor yard-stick. There was no sewer system in Greece at the time of Pericles. And yet that country produced Achilles, Sophocles, Euripides, Demosthenes-

And Gregoire.
