-in Shakespeare's days, yet England had a brilliant civilization in that era.
That is why I cannot understand how, when dealing with the water level in the harbour of Montreal and sewers, the discussion turned, with the help of the hon. member for York-Humber, to the civilization the people of Montreal want to show the world during Expo '67.
If the hon. member for York-Humber wants to learn something about civilization in Montreal, he should not look at the defects of the city's sewer system, but rather come to the Place des Arts to hear our symphony orchestra-
And St. Denis street.
Let him listen to the wonderful productions on the C.B.C. French network.
Hear, hear.

We could give him that opportunity by setting up a French television station of the C.B.C. in Toronto.
He might also attend plays staged by the many theatrical companies in Montreal, such as the Rideau Vert, the Theatre du Nou-veau-Monde, the Egregore, and others I forget. The hon. member would then really come in contact with the civilization of Montreal and of all Quebec, the one we would like to show the citizens of Toronto who will be good enough to visit Expo '67.


Mr. Chairman, it is not only for its civilization that Montreal should be admired and I feel the need to raise those issues. Headed by such a dynamic mayor as the present incumbent, Montreal has for years been developing at a clip and if more progress would be desirable in certain areas, I am sure this will shortly be taken care of, to the satisfaction of the hon. member for York-Humber.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, my speech today concerns another field.
You have not started yet?

I should like to address myself-and the hon. member for Levis may be glad I draw the minister's attention to this matter-to what I would call the unfair and even illegal competition carried on by the Canadian National Railways, with the encouragement of the Canadian government and the Department of Transport, against the private trucking industry in the province of Quebec and the whole of Canada.
The first objective of the C.N.R., when this company was established and work first undertaken, was to create an all-Canada coast-to-coast, railway system to unite the country, the various areas, the various provinces and municipalities and to set up passenger and freight service between all provinces, all areas and all municipalities in this country. This was the first objective of the creation of the C.N.R. to give the whole country services which other railway companies could not then provide.
Today, however, we see that the Department of Transport has given railway companies in Canada quite a different role. They are allowed, either the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. to give unfair competition to the trucking industry which is one of the major Canadian industries-I shall come back to this later.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)


companies are prohibited from going into the trucking business. The minister indicates that he is. But why is this allowed in Canada when elsewhere it is deemed to interfere with all normal, basic and logical cartel or combine legislation?
This is tolerated here and the C.N.R. takes advantage of it. And to think that in spite of everything, the company is unable to show a surplus; on the contrary, it shows a deficit that again must be covered by the Canadian taxpayers.
And what about shipping on the St. Lawrence. Mind you, railway companies, the Canadian Pacific in particular, all have merchant vessels they would be interested in operating up to Montreal in the winter. And why can they not? Because the federal government grants special subsidies for freight transport from the Maritimes to the centre of Canada. The C.P.R. and the C.N.R. are much more interested in getting special subsidies. The Canadian people pay taxes again for this, while the port of Montreal remains closed to shipping. Yet, winter shipping on the St. Lawrence up to Montreal is something possible nowadays, and it has been proven.
That would be progress not only for Montreal or Quebec but for all of Canada because then, the whole Canadian industry would benefit.
Let me give the following example of certain companies which are forced to spend considerable amounts of money to store their material in winter because they cannot ship it except in summer. It is well known that Canada is faced with fierce competition concerning the exportation of its natural resources such as asbestos, newsprint, aluminum and other products.
In the past, Canada filled nearly 90 per cent of Europe's asbestos requirements. Today, Russia has entered the asbestos market and Canada sells only 64 per cent of that commodity. Why? Because winter transportation is virtually impossible, unless you pay higher rates for shipments to the Maritimes. Therefore, producing companies would rather wait till summer to ship their merchandise, because doing it in winter, through the Maritimes, increases the cost and our Canadian industries can no longer compete with Russian industries which do not have to pay such transportation costs in the country.
The Aluminum Company of Canada, in its brief to the Gordon commission, pointed out that the sale of aluminum products had decreased on the export market due to increas-
Supply-Transport
ingly tougher competition from abroad; the Aluminum Company of Canada said further that shipping on the St. Lawrence in winter meant economies which enable those industries to win back lost ground on the world market.
Mr. Speaker, because the railway companies receive subsidies from the government-$10 million, $20 million-to transport freight from the Maritimes, they prefer to run their trains from the Maritime toward the central section of the country rather than help our industry compete with other countries in the matter of exports.
Those are the reasons, Mr. Chairman, which lead us to say that the present policy of the federal government and the transport department concerning subsidies for the transportation of freight by rail in Canada is no longer adequate, that it is even illogical, and that it is no help at all to the economy of the country because it is forcing into stagnation one of the most important Canadian industries, the trucking industry.
The sum of $20 million had been voted for one year in order to meet salary increases. Did the railway companies try to find a way to finance these salary increases when the $20 million would be gone? No. The $20 million were used to lower the rates, and after a year the railway companies came back to parliament for a further $20 million. This was granted in 1961 and I think another $20 million was voted; in other words, $50 million were added in 1964 and so we have this sum in the supplementary estimates "D" for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966. The amount of those subsidies, which stood at $20 million in 1958, has now reached $70 million. Where are we going at this rate? We might as well say that the federal government, the Department of Transport or the Canadian people are footing the bill for all [DOT] freight transportation in Canada, when private enterprise can do it at a reasonable price.
As I said, let us subsidize the C.N.R. where private enterprise cannot provide a service or so that it can lower its rates to the private enterprise level, but not to put them below that of private enterprise. It would certainly be illogical to have the federal government subsidize the railways to this end with the Canadian taxpayers' money.
You would think that the government was trying to ruin private enterprise which, through taxes, is filling the government's coffers.


Supply-Transport
Well, Mr. Chairman, in those circumstances, we want to protest against those many subsidies, against the government's way of doing those things, against the policy now followed by the Department of Transport.
It is time for a definite program to be submitted to the attention of all those who are looking after the transportation business in Canada, so that the Canadian trucking industry may know what to expect and what the future has in store for them.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the first opportunities members of the house have had for a long time to deal with the many problems that exist within the transportation industry in Canada today. There is so much involved in the administration of this department which requires the attention not only of the department but of the House of Commons and the entire transportation industry that one scarcely knows where to begin. A problem exists in respect of the railways with regard to both passenger and freight services. We have waited for several years for a specific statement on regional air policy. To date no such policy has been put forward. Another matter of importance is the MacPherson commission report and the changes to the Railway Act to be based on it. While many of these things are of paramount importance and have almost reached the position of being crises in this country, I should like to deal with railway transportation in respect of passenger service in part but in greater detail with regard to the lack of facilities for freight movement within Canada to-day.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
At the outset I say to the minister that I consider to be improper the supplementary judgment issued by the Board of Transport Commissioners within the last few days respecting the cancellation of the "Dominion". I say it is improper to hand down a supplementary judgment of this kind when the board knows very well that the original judgment is being appealed to the Governor in Council. Under section 53 of the Railway Act the Governor in Council is required to hear petitions of appeal and surely it is not going to be helpful to public relations with the people involved for a supplementary judgment to be issued by the Board of Transport Commissioners stating that they are not going to order the C.P.R. to reinstate this service even for the summer. What

makes it even more improper so far as I am concerned is that it is not a unanimous judgment. Commissioner Woodward has filed a minority report indicating that he does not agree there is justification for advising the C.P.R. at the present time that this passenger train service will not be required during the summer of 1966 or 1967.
Another problem that has arisen very recently is what is commonly referred to as the slow movement of grain from the western prairies to export position. I was amazed, indeed astounded, by the remark made in the house yesterday by the Minister of Finance who suggested he would not agree with the proposition that there has in fact been a slow movement of grain from the western prairies in this crop year. The minister suggested that recently the terminals in Vancouver have been unloading something like 600 cars per day. If that is true, and I accept it as being true, this has only happened very recently. It is unfortunate indeed in my opinion that the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board should in this house give aid and comfort to the railways when they have failed so miserably during this crop year to deliver grain into export position.
I have in my hand a statement from the Canadian Wheat Board respecting the quota distribution as at February 7, 1966, only three days ago. I am not going to go into all the details of this statement but it gives the figures for this crop year and the previous crop year for each of the provinces. In all the provinces as of this date there are still 108 shipping points on a two bushel per specified acre quota. On the same date last year there were none in that low category. On February 7 this year there were 303 shipping points on only three bushels per specified acre and a year ago there were only 31. On a four bushels per acre quota there were 498 shipping points as of February 7 this year and last year there were only 331.
When you look at the other end of the quotas, in other words, at the six bushels per acre shipping points, you find that as at February 7 last year there were 950 such points and this year there are 581 or about half as many. I think this gives an indication of the over-all situation in so far as moving grain out of western Canada is concerned. Quotas certainly have not risen as rapidly this year as they did last year. What is more, we were led to believe last fall that the sales of grain to China, Russia and many of our other customers were higher for this crop


year than last year, but the performance to date with regard to delivery is as I have stated.
However, Mr. Chairman, these figures do not tell the whole story. There are many points in southern Alberta that I know of-I could read these letters into the record if I had time-where, even though the very lowest quota has been set, namely, two bushels per acre, sufficient box cars have not been put into position to enable the farmers at these shipping points to deliver even that small amount. It goes further than that. I checked last night to make sure I was correct and was told that one of the flour mills in Medicine Hat now has placed over 200 orders for grain in the area. Yet we are told that mill orders are given priority. In one particular case an order was issued last October for a carload of grain and it came in last week. Therefore it is amazing and somewhat disappointing to hear the Minister of Finance say that as far as he knows there has been no slow movement of grain in western Canada.
Very recently I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the delay or slow movement of grain was interfering in any way with Canada's external aid program. The minister said, "I do not know that there is any problem at all". We received the same kind of answer again. I can tell the minister this. An order has now been issued by the Department of External Affairs, or whoever handles these matters, for some flour to be shipped to India and unless there is a remarkable change in the delivery of grain to the mills that will be gristing the flour the managers of the mills will simply throw up their hands and say they do not know where they are going to get the grain. Even today not sufficient grain is being hauled in to allow them to meet their commitments for domestic flour and the obligations they have with respect to the very large flour order received from Russia a few months ago.
I believe the time has long passed for some action in this regard. The Minister of Transport will have to take a far more active interest in what is happening to our railway transportation system. I say this, Mr. Chairman, because our railway transportation system is apparently gradually becoming more and more inadequate in keeping up with the present demands of our economy. We do not require any additional legislation to deal with this kind of problem. The Railway Act states very clearly that the minister and the Board of Transport Commissioners
Supply-Transport
have the authority, if they will use it, to require the railways to provide services and facilities for all the traffic that is offered to them. I am sure most hon. members are familiar with section 315 of the Railway Act. The obligation on the railways is set out very clearly in this section and I shall read part of it:
The company shall, according to its powers,
(a) furnish, at the place of starting, and at the junction of the railway with other railways, and at all stopping places established for such purpose, adequate and suitable accommodation for the receiving and loading of all traffic offered for carriage upon the railway;-
Section 315 (b) reads:
furnish adequate and suitable accommodation for the carrying, unloading and delivering of all such traffic;-
Then it says in paragraph (c):
without delay, and with due care and diligence, receive, carry and deliver all such traffic;-
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
That section of the Railway Act has not been repealed. It is still as valid as when it was written. I know of no attempt whatever by the Minister of Transport or by the Minister of Finance, who is responsible for the the Canadian Wheat Board, or by the Board of Transport Commissioners to order the Canadian Pacific to provide the cars that are required to haul the grain that is offered to them. Yet this is part of the law. It is not good enough to say that they do not know about these problems. If the Minister of Transport and other responsible ministers of the Crown are paying any attention whatever to the freight situation in western Canada, surely they must know that there has been a very unsatisfactory performance in so far as the railways are concerned, particularly the Canadian Pacific.
I think it should be unnecessary, Mr. Chairman, to remind the Minister of Transport of what the MacPherson Royal Commission had to say. One of the opening paragraphs of the report of that commission reads:
An adequate system for transporting men and material is a necessary condition of a modem industrial society.
Yet we have the situation that has developed over these last two or three years in which the railways are not meeting the demands for railway freight service. Apparently nothing is being done about it. I note that even in the United States there is talk about the problem of finding enough freight cars. For example, I have a press release dated


Supply-Transport
February 5 which indicates that Senator Burdick from North Dakota has introduced a bill in the United States Senate designed to help the railways resolve the freight car shortage which they term a national emergency.
However, Mr. Emerson, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway, appeared before the Board of Transport Commissioners and said that there were 9,200 Canadian Pacific box cars in the United States. Our own grain is lying in elevators and not being moved into an export position. Many ships waiting in harbour have had to leave because they could not wait longer. But there has been no action whatever on the part of the Minister of Transport even to attempt to use his influence on the railways to remedy the situation.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I think the time is long past when the Minister of Transport, if he is going to discharge the responsibilities he has to this nation, should take a very keen personal interest in this matter to see that the situation is corrected. It is not good enough to say that there is far more grain being offered now than there has been for some years and that the problem may be only temporary. This situation has occurred year after year and it is getting worse. What is worse, Mr. Chairman, is that as the demands of other freight traffic increase the Canadian Pacific seems to leave all the grain until everything else is hauled.
I do not believe that sort of attitude toward the handling of grain was ever anticipated when the millions of dollars and millions of acres of land were granted to the Canadian Pacific to undertake this job. I do not know how I can adequately impress upon the minister how serious this matter is. I urge him to do something about it. We could go back over the history of the conditions under which the Canadian Pacific was given land grants, concessions and so on. However, I assume that is well known to the minister. At least, I hope so.
One of the most amazing statements I have heard was made during a Board of Transport Commissioners' hearing when Mr. Emerson and Mr. Fraine, Vice President in charge of railway operations, were asked if the C.P.R. could haul additional tonnage on the fast freights which move in both directions through western Canada. They admitted it was possible to handle a substantial number of additional cars on these fast freights in so far as weight was concerned but they

categorically refused to give any consideration to hauling any grain on these trains because it would slow down their speed.
If we have reached a situation in Canada where the grain traffic is going to be set aside not only day after day but week after week and often even for months because the railway is too busy hauling something else, then I believe we have to conclude that the parliament of this country has to take some very positive action to correct this situation. We hope that the grain exports, which have been amounting to anywhere from 500 million to 600 million bushels, are going to continue. If we have gone beyond the amount that any particular railway is able to transport, then this will of course put a very firm ceiling on the amount of grain business we can do.
I am a little concerned about the statements by senior officials of the Canadian Pacific that they are not going to put grain on these fast freights. It seems to me that under the Railway Act the Board of Transport Commissioners has the authority to tell the railway to haul some grain on these trains. Section 323 of the act indicates that they have the authority but they certainly have not used it up until now. They have the authority to make sure there is no undue preference for any single kind of traffic. We had hoped, for example, when navigation on the lakes closed about December 15 that this situation would be resolved.
We had hoped that following the close of navigation there would be additional equipment available to move grain to the west coast. Even this has not happened. At least, there has been no apparant increase on Canadian Pacific lines. I hope the Minister of Finance is correct and that the situation has changed in the last few days. Representations have been made time after time to the responsible ministers about this whole problem. However, none of them seems to take an active interest in the problem with the exception of the Minister of Agriculture. When he made his trip to western Canada recently he seemed to be aware of the fact there was a problem; at least, he made some statements about it. There have been some remarks passed back and forth in the house to the effect that he had his wings clipped when he got back to Ottawa.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I hope that has not happened, Mr. Chairman. As I see the situation in western Canada, what the Minister of Agriculture said appeared to be closer to the truth than


what the Minister of f inance and the Minister of Transport have said with regard to the performance of the railroads so far in this *crop year. Therefore, we sincerely plead with the minister to take a keen interest in grain movement and do whatever he can to impress on the C.P.R. that Canada granted that railway its franchise and all its other concessions with the expectation that it would perform the duties and functions for which the railroad was built.
I do not want to take a lot of time in this extremely important debate and perhaps I can come back later to the question of passenger service, but I should like the minister to consider one or two matters before we reach the remainder of his estimates. So far as I am concerned the so-called variable costs respecting the "Dominion" supplied by the C.P.R. to the Board of Transport Commissioners hearings were simply not the kind of figures we expect so far as the public interest is concerned. Under cross-examination the officials were unable to give any clearcut indication of how much of these so-called variable costs would be saved if the "Dominion" did not run. It is interesting to note that at this hearing it was suggested that somewhere between 55 to 60 per cent of the so-called costs attributed to the operation of the "Dominion" would not be saved at all but would be continuing costs to the company whether or not the train ran.
A book published in 1935 by the University of Toronto Press and written by Professor W. T. Jackman says at page 101:
1.	That about 55 per cent of the operating expenses and about 65 per cent of the total expenses are constant and go on despite the changes in the amount of traffic carried by the railways.
2. That only about 45 per cent of the operating expenses and about 35 per cent of the total expenses vary in accordance with changes in the volume of traffic carried.
If you subtract 55 to 60 per cent of the so-called costs which the C.P.R. claimed as attributable to the "Dominion", then there is no deficit at all in operating that train. If there is no deficit, Mr. Chairman, I should like the Minister of Transport to know that I think the people of Canada are entitled to that passenger service. On the other side of the ledger, one thing which is very certain is that when you withdraw a service all the revenue disappears. If 55 to 60 per cent or around $10 million to $11 million, of the so-called variable costs are going to be continuing costs, then there is no justification in my mind, purely on the basis of costs, for allowing the C.P.R. to withdraw this service.
Supp ly-Transport
The other matter which disturbs me greatly about reducing railway passenger service is this. Canada has some great plans, at least, I hope we have, to celebrate our centennial in 1967. Last summer thousands of people got in touch with their members of parliament and claimed they could not get reservations on either the "Dominion" or the "Canadian" even though they had applied months in advance.
The C.P.R. deny this. But, of course, though they deny it they cannot prove the statement wrong because they have not been keeping track of the number of requests made for space. I think it is commendable that they have been ordered to make some attempt to keep track of requests for space. There has been a reduction in the number of people carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway as a result of discontinuing the "Dominion". During the summer this train hauled anywhere from 16 to 24 cars. By their action they are reducing by 50 per cent the number of people who could use this service in 1966 and 1967.
In 1967 we will also have Expo. We hope people from all over Canada will take part in this great Canadian show. But if in 1965 there was insufficient space for people to travel across the country by rail and air and one service is reduced by 50 per cent, surely this will hurt the kind of performance we would like to see Canada put on at this exhibition in 1967.
I urge the minister that immediately or as soon as possible he take under consideration the orders that have been issued by the Board of Transport Commissioners. I also suggest that he at least go so far as to order this service to be restored at once until the end of 1967 so that we will not be frustrated or in any way inhibited in celebrating our 100th anniversary and taking part in our great world fair.
We would not be asking the C.P.R. to bear any great financial burden if the service was restored because according to studies which have been made going back to 1935 most of these costs are going to continue anyway. This also raises the other problem of who is going to pay the costs. The captive freight shippers? For matters such as maintenance of way and so on it is obvious there will be no diminishing of cost.
In closing I want to urge the minister to give these matters serious consideration. I think he already has legal authority under the Railway Act to tell the senior manage-


Supply-Transport
ment of the railways, particularly of the C.P.R., that the government intends to see to it that railway service, both passenger and freight, adequate to meet the rising demand in our expanding economy is continued.
I also suggest that one of the major items which is holding back the expansion of our economy today is the bottleneck in railway freight traffic. I hope the minister will use all his influence to make the senior management of the C.P.R. understand that the government of Canada intends to see that it lives up to the agreements the company entered into when it was formed, which include providing adequate facilities and accommodation for all traffic offered to them. That is not being done today, Mr. Chairman.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I have chosen this occasion for my maiden speech because, with the house now considering the estimates of the Department of Transport, the current subject of examination and debate on this floor is the field of national activity about which my constituency is most exercised and unhappy at the present time. I speak, of course, of Winnipeg South and of transportation, two items which this winter, sir, if found together in the same sentence, are highly inflammable.
I rise on this occasion to make my maiden speech in this greatest of all Canadian institutions. May I at the outset extend to you my congratulations on your nomination to the position in this great chamber which you occupy. You have already demonstrated by the discharge of your role since this house went into committee a few days ago that we can look forward throughout this session when in committee to fair, judicious and efficient chairmanship. Your example of parliamentary conduct is of tremendous educative value to new members of the house like myself.
I do not intend to follow the familiar pattern of the maiden speechmakers and subject you and the members of the committee to a bland recitation of the tourists' guidebook to Winnipeg South. You have not the time for it, sir. The members of this committee do not have the time for it. I have not the time for it, and I can assure you that the citizens of Winnipeg South have not the time for it.
The citizens of Winnipeg South, through their elected representative in this chamber, are here on urgent business. They are here to complain that, possibly as a calculated aspect

of the transportation program being pursued by the present government of this country and certainly as a result of it, the city of Winnipeg is being phased right out of the Canadian transportation picture. Through the slow erosion of the once-powerful Air Canada complex in greater Winnipeg, through a breach of promise to Winnipeg with respect to the new Canadian-American bilateral air line agreement, and Anally with a decision to permit the Canadian Pacific Railway to discontinue its "Dominion" passenger service, the present federal government would appear to be doing its best to wipe Winnipeg right off the map in the air and on the ground.
That, at any rate, is the way it appears to the people of Manitoba in general and to the people of Winnipeg in particular at the present time. If anyone in this chamber thinks that I overstate the case, let him come to Winnipeg. Let him talk to our mayor and to our area mayors. Let him talk to the chairman of our metropolitan government, to our provincial government officials, to our Chamber of Commerce, to our representative businessmen and to our private citizens. Let him come out and attend with me public meetings such as the one I attended less than a month ago where reasonable, respected leaders of our community, who are normally quiet-spoken, joined together in one of the strongest and most vigorous protests in my experience in Winnipeg. The federal government's treatment of Winnipeg in so far as transportation development is concerned was castigated at that meeting in language as strong as language can possibly be and still remain within the realm of respectability.
It is not common to hear citizens and community leaders eschew restraint and complain as bitterly in my part of Canada as we are complaining today. Year in and year out, through the march of the decades in our nation's history, I submit that the Manitoban has been the quiet Canadian, loyal, productive, interested in the good of the whole nation. He has been the strong, silent type. It is precisely because we have always been quiet that some in this chamber may think we shall always remain so.
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that if they think so they are living in a politician's paradise. I am here to state for the citizens of Winnipeg South, without equivocation, that where the broad national subject of transportation is concerned our sentiment is aroused and our patience is at the breaking point. Should we forgo our customary restraint,


should we regularly complain noisily and tediously about our lot in the national picture, and should we cry out in most un-Manitoban fashion, would it be so disloyal and destructive of us? Would it be necessarily wrong? The cry of outrage, of wounded pride, has worked for others in our Canadian confederation. Why should it not work for Manitoba too? Perhaps we only betray ourselves in Manitoba by being the quiet Canadians and by being reasonable.
We Manitobans want a place in what Premier Duff Roblin has called "the Canadian sun." Absolutely indispensable to the achievement of that goal is a place in the Canadian transportation picture befitting the size, the status, the economic requirements and the strategic, geographic location of the capital city of Winnipeg, which is a metropolitan community of half a million persons.
I find it incomprehensible, Mr. Chairman, that the present federal government should reason, as it quite obviously does, that it is perfectly sane Canadianism to build this country entirely on certain of its regions while ignoring other regions altogether. To me that is folly. What other country in the world of any status was built this way? However, worse than folly, sir, it is un-Canadian. The transportation program that this government is following is a deliberate policy of regional negligence of the most flagrant kind.
Hear, hear.

When we say in Manitoba that we desire a place for our province in the "Canadian sun" we are preaching Canadianism of the purest kind. For we also desire a place in the Canadian sun for Nova Scotia, for Prince Edward Island, for Saskatchewan, for the Yukon, for Quebec, and for every part of this great land whose potential is limited only by the limitations of man.
This is what we want in Manitoba and for Canada in all her parts. The people of each part must be strong if the nation is to be strong. More than that, each one of the parts has the right to be strong. And where one part is comparatively weak the rest of us are weak. The federal government has a sacred Canadian responsibility to contribute to the strengthening of all our parts. If the Atlantic provinces are strong, then I as a Canadian am the stronger for it. If they are weak, then I am the weaker. If the prairies are rich, then I as a Canadian am richer. If they are poor, then I am the poorer. This is our philosophy in Winnipeg. It is absolutely inconceivable to
Private Bills
us that the present Canadian government should think and act otherwise. Mr. Chairman, I have considerably more to say but I am watching the clock. May I call it six o'clock?

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Richard for the second reading of Bill No. C-lll, to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada.

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hour for private members' business expired the last time this bill was being considered, I had had little more than an opportunity to indicate that I felt that the subject matter of Bill C-lll, which is designed to achieve the incorporation of the Bank of Western Canada, was a very important one. I indicated at that time that I might have something to say on the subject when it came before us again.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I do not wish to delay the house unduly in its consideration of this matter but there are one or two comments I should like to make. I think there has been growing recognition in this parliament during the last couple of years of the important role which it might be possible for regional banks to play in developing the economy of our country. The arguments put forward in respect of this particular application include a claim that the bank

February 10, 19G6
Private Bills
in respect of which this application is made will serve as a new regional bank. Those who advocate it have seen fit to bestow upon this proposed new bank the title "Bank of Western Canada" and provision is made for the head office to be situated in Winnipeg. I realize it has become something of a habit among a number of members of this house to think of the city of Winnipeg as being in western Canada. Representing as I do Co-mox-Alberni in this house, let me say that Winnipeg seems to me a long way from western Canada.
I realize that this question has been a topic of discussion over the years. So far as I am concerned Winnipeg is in central Canada. I think one has only to look at a map of our country to realize that this is the situation. Geographically speaking, it is roughly in the centre of Canada. I suggest, therefore, that this proposed bank might much better be described as "the Bank of Central Canada" rather than "the Bank of Western Canada". If I were to look through my files I believe I could produce what amounts to official recognition on the part of the government of Canada of this proposition. Recently I was in conversation on this question with some of my hon. friends who represent the city of Winnipeg in this chamber and I was finally able to produce to them a government publication entitled "The Climate of Central Canada". We discovered on examining this publication that it was describing the climate in and around the city of Winnipeg.
The point I am making is strengthened by the fact that the bill as it now stands provides that the directors of the proposed bank shall be residents of Canada but no mention is made of the area in which they should reside. Those who are interested in this bill, the provisional directors, are in fact residents of the city of Toronto. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that after perusing the bill carefully I am somewhat sceptical that this proposed bank is in fact designed to be a regional bank even for the region around the city of Winnipeg, quite apart from the question I raised earlier concerning the name of the bank, which might not be too important.
It might be of interest to point out in this connection that as we all know another proposal for a new regional bank has been introduced in the other place. I understand, in fact, that it has been given second reading there. I refer to the application by the proposed Bank of British Columbia. It is interesting to note that under the terms of

that bill, as contrasted with the one before us, it is provided that a majority of the directors must be resident in the province of British Columbia. I think this is an important distinction to be drawn if one is thinking in terms of the functioning of regional banks.
When this question was being considered earlier we heard a fairly lengthy speech from the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis). I listened to it attentively because I was interested in his argument. At that time I was disposed to pursue some of the remarks he made. However, on reflection I felt most of his observations were addressed to the application on behalf of the Bank of British Columbia which I have just mentioned. He dealt at some length with the question whether or not provincial governments should be allowed to hold shares in chartered banks. I consider this to be an important matter for debate although I am not so sure that this is an appropriate time for such a debate to take place.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano went to such length in dealing with this particular question, however, that I feel I should say something about it. I have not altered the views I held when similar applications were before us. Indeed, I believe the proper functioning of regional banks in the interests of the development of the whole of Canada might be more effective if the interested government authorities in the provinces or regions concerned were entitled to have some say as to the way in which these banks were run. Contrary to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, such an interest in these banks would in no way weaken the jurisdiction of the federal government and parliament of Canada over monetary and fiscal matters. Indeed, it might serve to ease some of the existing strains which occur under our present constitution in relations between the federal and the provincial levels of government.
I know that in the other place an assurance has been given by the hon. Senator sponsoring the bill in question. He stated he had been authorized by the Premier of British Columbia to give an undertaking that the provincial government would not seek to hold any shares in that or any other chartered bank. I much regret that the Premier of British Columbia has backed off from the position he took earlier in this connection. I believe this will weaken the effectiveness of the development of regional banking in the area.


[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I understand that the application of the other bank has been allowed to go to the banking and commerce committee of the other place. Bearing in mind the history of some of these banking applications introduced in the past, I am inclined to assume that Their Honours will allow this particular application to come to this house for our consideration. That being the case, the detailed consideration of all the aspects which are raised by these two applications could be undertaken by our Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when representations from all of the parties involved could be heard. For that reason I am quite agreeable to this bill receiving second reading today.

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not forgive myself if I did not take this opportunity to say a few words on the economic and banking situation in Canada. Yesterday I listened to the hon. members who criticized the banks and tried to prove to us that more banks were needed to increase competition between these institutions, which would be of great benefit to the people.
I do not quite share the views of hon. members who say that one or two more banks, even a few more, would create more competition in Canada and would serve Canadians better.
I say to these hon. members that all these institutions are governed by the same regulations and that they would charge the same interest rates. One bank more or less would not put more money in circulation. A few banks more or less will not make much difference in the country's economic situation, or consumption in Canada. Banks are good and solid institutions which must be preserved; we are not against banks but rather against the great powers which the nation's supreme authorities have entrusted to them.
Banks rule the roost in Canada. Individuals, governments, public bodies have to bow to them for such credit as they receive in dribs and drabs. Those great institutions are in need of reform, and if we create other banks or near-banks on the same system, with the same powers, we will be no further ahead.
Some financial reforms should be made. As I was saying a moment ago, banks are not concerned with consumption. If someone wants to borrow money from them, they will lend it to him according to the confidence 23033-65
Private Bills
they have in him. If they have confidence in an individual or if this individual owns property or has any collateral, his credit will be good at the bank. But they do not take consumption into account. If the only basis to obtain a loan in such institutions is the confidence they have in a few people, then I will say that these institutions can have confidence in only about 10 per cent of the Canadian people. This means that 90 per cent of the citizens cannot use the services of or obtain loans from these institutions.
Those institutions are unwilling to meet the needs of Canadians and take no account of consumption or overproduction in Canada. That is why we ask the government and members of the house to take their responsibilities. We know that everything is going well in Canada, we have nothing to complain about production, because it is abundant in every field, but distribution is not taking place. This is so because there is not enough purchasing power in the hands of the citizens, and it is up to the government to see that those institutions serve our people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those institutions are powerful. They are so strong and powerful that the government itself and hence, the Minister of Finance, must beg them for the credit required to finance the country.
These institutions create credit at will. They manufacture the finances and the credit of the country, but this credit is manufactured only in the form of indebtedness. They create credit by incurring debts and when the supposedly sovereign nation needs credit, it is required to incur debts and bow to these great institutions and submit to them, in order to secure the credit required to finance and administer the country.
Major reforms are needed, Mr. Speaker, and if we are in debt as we are today, those are the institutions that put Canada into debt, the individuals into debt, the companies into debt because there is not one cent circulating that does not bear interest; in fact, there is not a cent in circulation, now in the hands of the taxpayers, that is not repayable. This money must be repaid, and the banks have the advantage of making this credit, of lending it to the nation, of lending to individuals in the form of interest. But as those institutions do not lend interest, they must be repaid a capital that they have not created or that they have not lent; that is the reason why we are always short of capital and we are not able to finance the nation-

As I was saying a moment ago, there is not much that is wrong in Canada, except the credit system, which does not serve the country, does not finance institutions and industries, but only finance by creating debts, and that is why we ask the government to assume its responsibilities.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
New credit should be created by the Bank of Canada or by a control institution in Canada, independently of the chartered banks-

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about that bill, it seems to me that I am within the limits of the debate, because these are financial institutions which exercise control over the nation. When there is talk of granting other bank charters or of setting up other institutions to fleece the nation in the same fashion, it seems to me something should be said or done so that at least some members of parliament might learn how those institutions function.
Mr. Speaker, a lot could be said about banks, but I shall limit myself to saying that we must, at all costs, assume some responsibilities and modernize our financial institutions; they are as old as the world and have never been reformed. We have accepted all kinds of mechanical and technical developments; we have accepted science and progress in all spheres, but we have never accepted any reforms in the financial field.
So, to be up to date, the need to reform these institutions must be recognized and they must be given adequate powers. Not a free hand though, because the government must keep the main powers, particularly the power to create credit. Thus the government could finance the nation, all the institutions in Canada, and use part of this credit to finance public assets bridge and road construction, in short, to finance various public projects, such as universities and schools, using free-interest money.
Mr. Speaker, those are the suggestions I wanted to put before the house. If they were accepted, millions of dollars would be saved for the taxpayers. Some purchasing power would be left to the taxpayers who could provide for their own needs, develop their industries, their natural resources, in a word, develop a great deal of things, if only they were left some purchasing power.
But since all this money is debt money that has to be repaid in excess of the amount received, it is impossible for our people to grow, to fulfil themselves and to develop their own natural resources. That is why 85 per cent of Canada's natural resources are being developed by foreigners.

That an order of the house do issue for copies of all the working papers prepared for the Norris commission by the chartered accountants hired by the commission and deposited by Mr. Justice Norris with the Department of Labour.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to debate this motion in the detail I would have if it had come up for discussion last session when I first proposed it. I say that because it should be obvious to everyone in the house and the people of Canada generally that the problems of the waterfront and the Seafarers' International Union are not of as urgent importance as they were, or at least the public does not consider them to be so. At the same time, I think it is important to establish certain facts.
In 1963 parliament passed, by an overwhelming majority of the members then in the house, legislation to establish a Board of Maritime Trustees with the authority and responsibility of supervising in great detail the operations of a number of unions which
23033-65J

had been established in the maritime industry. For many of us who have worked with and for labour for years this was a difficult vote. The labour movement on the North American continent has historically and traditionally been voluntary and operates without very much day to day supervision by outside forces, including government.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I think this is a good way. On the whole it has worked very well. Many of us who voted for the legislation which established the Board of Trustees did so only because we had become convinced that it was necessary. Let us look at the facts which were brought out and which convinced us that this legislation was necessary. Over the years there had been a whole series of acts of violence, arson, beatings and possibly murder on the waterfront. When the labour movement found it impossible to deal with the S.I.U., headed in those days by Hal Banks, they appealed to the Conservative government of that time to take some action. The government was loath to do so or found it difficult to do so.
Finally the union workers who operated the Welland Canal closed that canal to shipping. Only then did the government act. A commission was appointed under Mr. Justice Norris to look into the whole question of the waterfront and the unions operating thereon. I do not have to tell members of this house what Mr. Justice Norris found. I do not have to tell members of this house that he found that the S.I.U., headed by Mr. Banks, had been guilty of acts of violence, beatings, arson and other illegal actions. It was then that the house was asked to vote on the legislation I have mentioned.
Mr. Banks is probably as bad as everything that has been said about him and possibly worse, but he could not have done those things unless he had received the co-operation of very influential and important organizations outside the labour movement. When we discussed the passage of the legislation establishing the Board of Maritime Trustees I pointed out that Mr. Banks had the most intimate connections with shipping companies, particularly with one very large shipping company, Canada Steamship Lines. I pointed out the connections which he had with other organizations and which he must have certainly had with political figures in the areas in which his union operated.
During the course of that debate and subsequently it became apparent that some very


Motion for Papers
interesting information was available in the working papers which had been prepared for the Norris Commission by its accountants amongst others. I laid a motion before the house last session asking that these papers be tabled. The position taken by the government was that they were private documents, that they were the property of the commission and the government ought not to table them.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the government's position that if civil servants and people who work for the government have to worry that every time they put something on paper it will be raised in the House of Commons, they may be very loath to write what they think and give opinions. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of sympathy for that position, but I find it difficult to understand why the government refuses to permit the tabling of these documents when the government or somebody very high up-I must assume it was the former Minister of Labour-permitted a reporter for the Toronto Daily Star to spend what obviously must have been some considerable time in the Department of Labour going through the very documents which the government refuses to table and using the information he obtained to write a very long article.
I shall put on record some of the things this reporter said in his article because it will indicate why I believe it is important, first of all, that the government agree to table these documents and, second, why I think the people of Canada have a right and in fact would be extremely interested to know what these documents contain. I quote from the Toronto Daily Star of November 6, 1964. There is a long article on page 1 written by Robert Reguly, Star staff writer. The headline is "Banks Files Show Funds To 6 Liberals". I shall read just a few paragraphs of this article:
Hal Banks' Seafarers International Union issued cheques to the political agents of five Montreal area Liberal candidates just before the 1962 federal election, The Star has learned.
The union also contributed to the 1957 campaign of a former Liberal M.P. for a New Brunswick riding.	.
Evidence of the contribution was unearthed in S.I.U. files by investigators for the Norris commission-the government inquiry that last year slammed the S.I.U. and Banks' despotic rule . . .
The evidence of S.I.U. political contributions was never made public. The Norris inquiry shied away from revealing the S.I.U.'s political entanglements . . .
tMr. Orlikow.l
But references to these political payments also crop up in the confidential working papers of the Norris commission's financial investigators.
These working papers are in the federal Labour Department files and this reporter has seen them and made transcripts of them.
The papers, largely handwritten, were culled by Norris investigators from the books of the S.I.U. and its auditors.
Then this purports to be a quotation from these papers:
"Plain white voucher dated May 31, 1957, cheque 0711, paid to (naming a former Liberal M.P.) contribution to campaign of above for Member of Parliament in election (naming a New Brunswick riding). Amount of $1,000".
Working paper numbered H12, listing "six political contributions June, 1962".
Five of the contributions referred to were in the form of S.I.U. cheques, of about $1,000 each, paid to the official agents of five Montreal-area Liberal candidates just before the election that brought the Liberals back into power.
Later in the same article Mr. Reguly says: Besides referring to specific payments to the agents of individual candidates for the Commons, Norris investigators noted "an astronomical rise" in union legal fee payments at federal election times.
I could go on and on in this vein, Mr. Speaker. I am not suggesting for one moment that it was wrong for the S.I.U. to make contributions to political parties. I would hope that more trade unions would adopt the policy of business organizations, become interested in politics and make contributions to party funds. I do not care to which party they make a contribution. They have a right to make a contribution to any political party they prefer, provided of course they make it in the way which is permitted under the union constitution, namely by making a recommendation to the local unions, having the recommendation passed in the normal way and so on. I have no objection to that being done because it is their business.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I think they waste their money when they make contributions to Liberal candidates but that is their business if they do it in the right way. But today I am concerned with the problem I raise, the tendency of this government to declare private practically every document. I shall not go into detail this evening, but I have another motion on the order paper asking for the tabling of the working papers presented to the conference on the war on poverty. That motion has been turned down because it is said that these documents are private. When that motion is being debated I will come into this house with ten sets of these documents because you can get them


any time you want by just calling the people who were at the conference. This illustrates how ridiculous this whole question of secrecy is. I will discuss that question on another occasion.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I do not ask for any special rights for myself or any other member of parliament but surely members of parliament are entitled to the same rights and privileges as are given to anybody else. I do not know whether the Toronto Star reporter gained access to those documents because he is Liberal; I do not know whether he gained access to them because if he did not get access he would have raised other matters which might have been embarrassing to the Liberal party. But, Mr. Speaker, from the few quotations I have put on the record tonight from this article it is obvious that Mr. Reguly was given access to these documents. I suggest to members of this house that no newspaper reporter should have a right to peruse, study and quote from documents which the government claims are private and which are refused to members of parliament. It is for that reason I have moved this motion.

subtopic: NORRIS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) I too was caught unawares since I did not believe I would be speaking on this particular motion tonight. The hon. member made several interesting points which I believe we will have an opportunity to refute in the two hours and forty minutes available to debate such a motion.
I was particularly interested in the hon. member's declared interest in the labour movement. I should like to go on the record also by pointing out to the hon. member that an interest in the labour movement is not necessarily confined to the New Democratic party. I can remember my first pay cheque when I was 17 years of age. It was exactly $18.10 and I spent $15 of that amount to join a labour union. I still remember it as a fine, venerable organization. I too share the hon. member's respect and admiration for the labour movement.
In his opening remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg North cast reflections upon the particular union which Mr. Banks happened to head at the time in question. I do not want to get into the story of Hal Banks. This motion does not lend itself to that, although the hon. member used it quite skilfully as a pretext to discuss Hal Banks and the Liberal
Motion for Papers
party. When the hon. member has an opportunity tomorrow to look through Hansard and weigh his own words he will find he has contradicted himself. I am only speaking from memory, and I apologize if I am wrong, but I believe he suggested that a reporter from the Toronto Star, with the permission of the then minister of labour, was permitted to peruse the working papers of the Norris Commission.
If we presume this to be true, then we give the minister very little credit for intelligence. I think we would be inclined to treat the minister a little more liberally than that. If the Liberal party did anything to be ashamed of in the way of alleged contributions, it hardly seems likely that a man of the calibre of the minister of labour of that time would invite a newspaper reporter, regardless of whether he was pro or anti-Liberal, to peruse documents and allow him to print at will short extracts from those working papers which might be embarrassing to the Liberal party. This is one point the hon. member made that seemed to me to be a little bit paradoxical.
He ended up his speech on the rather sanctimonious note that a union should be entitled to support the party of its choice. I do not believe any of us disagree with that. As a matter of fact, I am one of those who believe that the unions of this country are entitled to no less privileges than are other segments of industry, particularly private industry. When the chips are down I must confess I have always been regarded as pro labour in my sentiments.
If the hon. member believes that labour unions are entitled to make contributions to political parties, then I do not quite understand what he is concerned about if the union in question at the time made political contributions to any particular party, ours or his own. I should like to bring to his attention that the Norris Commission was established in July, 1962, by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) who was a very fine, decent minister of labour at whom nobody could throw stones, a man of integrity. If the S.I.U. in the early part of the campaign in 1962 saw fit to make election contributions to any member in the Montreal area, then I think it was the prerogative of the particular union in question. I resent the implication of the hon. member for Winnipeg North that the unions in those days had any less prerogatives than the C.B.R.T. which contributed very helpfully to the New Democratic Party. I for one as a


Motion for Papers
labour man am getting a little tired of the sanctimonious attitude of the people in that particular corner of the house when they indicate they have some particular prerogatives and privileges in connection with labour.
Since the hon. member is one of my favourites, Mr. Speaker, may I say there are some of the things he said with which I agree. I refer to the lack of clarity in the House of Commons in connection with the policy for the production of papers. I do not want to contradict myself but the other evening I had the opportunity of pointing out that the British system is that all documents are considered private unless they are by statute specifically declared to be public. Sweden, I said, had adopted the opposite principle, a more healthy approach, that all documents were public unless declared by decree to be private. I thought it was perhaps time that a committee of this house studied our whole attitude toward the question of the production of papers. I join with the hon. member in this regard, provided that was an aspect of the topic which he discussed. The reason he advanced the other afternoon when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) refused to table the documents was that he did not want to feel like a second class citizen inasmuch as the reporter from the Toronto Star had access to this file. I have some sympathy with this argument.
However, two wrongs do not make a right, Mr. Speaker. The investigations I have been able to make indicate that the reporter in question had access to the files but certainly not with the knowledge of the Minister of Labour. As I pointed out earlier, if there was anything in these documents that might have been embarrassing to the Liberal party it was hardly conceivable that the minister of labour of that day would want a reporter or reporters to have easy access to these working papers. If there was some doubt in my mind in connection with the notice of motion we discussed last week as to the advisability of producing papers, particularly because we did not have anything more than the jurisprudence or an affinity to the traditions of the British parliamentary system as a basis for automatically refusing production-I may differ from my party in this respect-of documents in response to reasonable requests, I think that in this particular case we do have definite guidelines set down whether or not the working papers of the Norris Commission should be made public.

As the hon. member pointed out, the Norris Commission was established in July, 1962, by the then minister of labour, the present member for Ontario. It was established by Order in Council based on a statute known as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which was passed in 1948 and possibly has had some amendments since that time. The report of the industrial inquiry into the disruption of shipping states very clearly at the outset the authority of the government in establishing that particular commission.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
As I understand it, not only from reading the book but on advice from the department, the industrial inquiry commission, generally known as the Norris Commission, concerning matters relating to the disruption of shipping on the Great Lakes was established pursuant to section 56 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Subsection 5 of section 56 refers to the provisions of sections 33 and 34 as applying mutatis mutandis which means "with necessary changes", for the benefit of the legal minds here, to an industrial inquiry commission I might say that not being a lawyer I had to spend a few hours finding out what this was all about. I was too bashful to ask the Minister of Labour.
I discovered that section 33 authorizes an inquiry commission to summon witnesses and require them to give evidence on oath. The section further provides that the information obtained from documents required to be produced shall not, except as the commission deems expedient, be made public.
A lot of generalities are involved when we talk about papers. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) had my general sympathy with his arguments the other evening. I think we are too secretive and too general about the production of papers. It impedes the work not only of the Opposition but also of responsible members on this side who like to know what goes on from time to time behind closed doors. But until such time as this house sets out clearly and concisely what documents are public and what documents are private we will have to proceed on almost an ad hoc basis of deciding through this medium of notices of motion which documents are public and which are private.
However, in the particular instance at hand there is no difficulty in my humble opinion. We can refer with some authority to a particular act, the Industrial Relations and


Supply-Tansport
Disputes Investigation Act. I should like to refer to subsection 5 of section 56 and in doing so I compliment the then minister of labour for the very broad terms he set out for the benefit, among others, of Judge Norris.
Before I refer to the section I will say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North that his opening remarks, in which he was fair and kind enough to admit that the general public is no longer concerned about disruption on the water front, are a definite indication that the trustees appointed as a result of the Norris Commission are doing a job for the country and doing it well.
