Mr. Chairman, I was saying when we broke for private members' hour that our philosophy in my part of the country, Manitoba, with respect to Canada is that of a total concept of Canada that embraces the idea that what is good for one part of the country is good for all the country and that what is bad for one part of the country hurts all of the country. I was saying that if the Atlantic provinces, for example, are strong, then I as a Canadian am the stronger for it. If they are weak, then I am the weaker. If the prairie provinces are rich, then I as a Canadian, sir, am the richer for it. And I asked if they are poor, am I not the poorer?
This is our philosophy in Winnipeg South, Mr. Chairman, and it is absolutely inconceivable, as I said, that the present Canadian government should think and act otherwise.
In a country such as ours, a continent wide, disparately settled, swept by winter, the transportation network has from the beginning been, and through the foreseeable future will continue to be, the most vital artery of our national body. Transportation and the total national transportation facility is the single most germane ingredient to the concept of Canada. Yet here is a government in Ottawa today that is so preoccupied with richer, more vociferous sections of the country, so concerned with its own nest, that the fourth largest metropolitan community in the country, the whole central plexus of geographical Canada, is left to wither and rot on the transportation vine.
What kind of policy for Canada is this, Mr. Chairman? Surely everyone in Canada would be better off if Manitoba were permitted and encouraged to play its rightful role in our national transportation environment. We must insist that we are not being parochial when we make such a legitimate demand. On the contrary, it is demonstrably in the national interest to let us do so.
The factor that militates most severely against Winnipeg and against Manitoba from a transportation point of view is the lack of an air policy in this country at the present time. There is no regional air policy in Canada. In fact, there is no national air policy, and the formulation of such a policy is a first priority requirement in our view.
In the United States the decision was wisely taken long ago to promote the growth of strong, regional air carriers. Today, 11 of the 13 such carriers in the United States are
[The Chairman.]
operating in the black, and far from siphoning off the profits of the larger air lines they are actually helping to develop traffic for them. With the big, highly expensive aircraft in use today by the large air lines, and the "fly over" system that these big air lines must necessarily employ, the development of healthy regional carriers is the only solution for the transportation needs of smaller Canadian centres, and the most realistic method of serving the public on relatively short distance runs.
Regional carriers such as TransAir Limited of Winnipeg need the support of the federal government if they are going to make the contribution to Canada that they are capable of making. They need a regional air policy, spelled out by Ottawa, that will put an end to the present Air Canada monopoly, and define territories for them in which they will have an opportunity to make a reasonable profit.
The unfortunate truth of the matter is that in Canada today there is, as I said before, no national air policy. There is only an Air Canada policy. Air Canada is an excellent air line, sir, with an enviable record, and it is dear to the hearts of Winnipegers because, as the old Trans-Canada Air Lines it was born in our city. But I suggest that to repose the air policy of this country in a government owned aerial monolith is a practice that is becoming more and more harmful to our economic growth. There is room for both. There is room for Air Canada and for the regional air carrier.
Mr. Chairman, a single, simple glance at the map of North America will reveal to anyone the reason for Winnipeg's current dissatisfaction with national transportation planning in this country. We are so located, geographically, that we should be the hub of continental air traffic. However, because of the policies of the present government we have nothing to show for it. Again, we are so located geographically that we should also be the hub of Canadian rail traffic. But because of the announced policies of the present government, and I refer specifically to the decision to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to cancel the "Dominion", we appear shortly doomed to find ourselves in a position where we have less of this type of economic enterprise than ever before in our recent history. Is it any wonder that public sentiment in our part of the country is aroused? Located where we are, and the home of a potentially formidable regional air carrier in


the corporate entity of TransAir Limited, we should be, in Winnipeg, the focus of a major air traffic enterprise fanning out in all directions to serve our developing northland, to serve Saskatchewan to the west, to serve northwestern Ontario to the east, and to serve the upper United States mid-west to the south.
We were assured by the Minister of Transport during the recent federal election campaign that no new bilateral air agreement would be signed with the United States until the Canadian negotiators secured what they wanted for Winnipeg.

Mr. Chairman, I know that the hon. gentleman does not mean to mislead with respect to what I said, but I never made any such statement, and any press report I have ever seen, although it had a statement like that in it, had a previous statement by me in quotation marks. That statement was a paraphrase of something I was supposed to have said but did not say.
That is a question of privilege.

Mr. Chairman, I might remark on that point that this was a specific quotation attributed to the minister, and perhaps attributed erroneously, but none the less attributed to the minister by a Winnipeg newspaper, the politics of which generally tend to favor the position of the party to which he belongs. It was a bylined signed article, and I have a clipping of that article in my file. However, I appreciate that one can be misquoted in the newspapers. Nevertheless the impression was created, and I subsequently wrote to the Minister of Transport with respect to this particular statement and received a gracious and lengthy reply from him.
The impression was created in Winnipeg that the minister had said that no new bilateral air agreement would be signed with the United States until the Canadian negotiators secured what they wanted for Winnipeg. If the minister says that he did not say that, then I suggest his position in Winnipeg has been compromised due to the tenor in which he was erroneously quoted in Winnipeg newspaper reports.
What was wanted for Winnipeg and by Winnipeg was a Winnipeg-Minneapolis-Chicago route for a Canadian carrier. Eight weeks after the election, an election which as we all know failed to go well for government
Supply-Transport
candidates in our region of the country, the terms of the new bilateral agreement were announced. Need anyone ask what they contained? They contained the customary plums for Montreal; the customary plums for Toronto; the customary gravy for the United States, and nothing at all for the west.
Hear, hear.

I refrain, Mr. Chairman, from drawing the cynical inference from this chain of events that must appear obvious to everyone in this chamber. Suffice it to say that in Winnipeg we just do not believe, somehow, that the Canadian negotiators tried very hard. We say, further, that if they did not want the Winnipeg-Minneapolis-Chicago run for Air Canada, and there is good reason to believe that they did not want it, they should have gone after it for TransAir. If they could not get it for TransAir, they should have insisted that Northwest Air Lines, the American carrier now enjoying monopoly status, start servicing the route properly.
We have heard the argument that there is not enough traffic from Winnipeg to Chicago to justify direct air service. Mr. Chairman, that will not wash. That is like saying there was not sufficient western traffic 90 years ago to justify the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Hear, hear.

Give us the route, Mr. Chairman, and let us tell businessmen in Winnipeg, Brandon, Regina, Saskatoon, Moose Jaw, Prince Albert, Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat that they need no longer go thousands of miles out of their way to reach the United States midwest, that all they need to do is fly direct to Winnipeg, and on to Chicago, and we will prove to you sir, that there is enough traffic to justify it.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
There is not enough traffic going from Winnipeg to Chicago via Minneapolis right now, to be sure, because up to the present time the service offered by Northwest Airlines has been of the milk-run type-far short of the standard the average business executive demands.
This is only one feature of the framework of frustration and discontent in which Winnipeg finds itself today where air transportation is concerned. We have-as I mentioned earlier-watched in bitterness and dismay


Supply-Transport
while the federal government has pursued a slow but inexorable transfer of our main Air Canada facilities to Montreal. Despite repeated assurances to the contrary, and throughout the long and acrimonious wrangle over the transfer of our Viscount overhaul base, Air Canada has continued to move skilled technical personnel out of Winnipeg at the rate of several families every month. This has been done while our local government, our citizens, Air Canada the federal government-all of us-have been waiting for the report of the Thompson Royal Commission on Winnipeg's air future.
Our provincial government was told early in January by the Minister of Transport that the Thompson report would be available no later than the end of January. Well, January has come and gone, and the report has not yet appeared. I can appreciate that it is often difficult to know the specific date by which such reports are likely to be issued. But my point is that the end of January has gone by, and the report is still awaited-which is understandable-but the transfers of personnel continue to take place.
I would ask the government in this same connection: Why is Winnipeg discriminated against when it comes to fixing the fares on international air routes? Why are we not permitted to take advantage of our geographical position when it comes to the rate structure? As a case in point, the one-way Air Canada fare from Montreal to Glasgow is $242. The one-way Air Canada fare from Winnipeg to Glasgow-a substantially shorter run-is $305. That is a surcharge of $63, yet the Winnipeg-Glasgow route goes over Hudson Bay and is therefore much shorter.
It costs more to fly to Europe from Winnipeg than to fly to Europe from Montreal, though it is a shorter route from our city. Why are we not permitted to take advantage of our geography-which works against us in so many other contexts-and to set up our city and our airport as the jump-off point to Europe for all the myriad tourists and business travellers in the central part of Canada and in the north central United States? If we could offer the lower fares that we are entitled to through our geography, we could capture that traffic and attract thousands of travellers annually to our city, to say nothing of offering our own citizens the lower fares to which they are legitimately entitled on their own overseas trips.

The federal government says we cannot do that because the fares on international air routes are fixed by IATA-the International Air Transport Association-and IATA bases its formula on rates to what it calls normal ports of entry, in this case Montreal. Why Montreal should be considered a more normal port of entry than Winnipeg in the mid-twentieth century, the air age, is a distinction the fine points of which escape us in western Canada completely. We are hardly back in the days of sail, although the Minister of Transport appears to be trying to put us there. The result of this archaic, anachronistic and discriminatory formula is that if you wish to fly from Winnipeg to Europe, you pay a fare which is the same as it would be if you flew from Winnipeg to Montreal and then flew from Montreal to Europe. That is the way the formula works, Mr. Chairman, and the government throws up its hands and says: We can't do anything about it; it's IATA.
Well, out west we do not take kindly to such transparent excuses. Why cannot the federal government do something about it? This is the Canadian government is it not? It helps shape IATA policy. What is the matter with us in Winnipeg? Are we not part of the Canadian government's responsibility? Are we not a part of Canada too? In the view of the federal government the answer to that question would appear to be no.
Figures reported in the Winnipeg newspapers just yesterday disclose the rate of growth currently to be lower in Winnipeg than in any other major city in the country. This is our condition at the moment and we place much of the blame for this squarely on the shoulders of the federal government and specifically the Department of Transport. The policies of the department are strangling us economically; strangling us and suffocating us.
The catalogue compiled by this federal government, where Winnipeg's transportation status is concerned, is a catalogue of dissembling and broken faith, a policy that flies in the face of all the lofty pronouncements about Canadian unity and co-operative federalism. Mr. Chairman, there are many suggestions I plan to make in this chamber in the weeks ahead with respect to development of major transportation facilities in Manitoba. But that is another story, and time does not permit my telling it today. What I have said today is for the record. It is my constituency's formal indictment of the transportation policy of regional partisanship that is being

pursued by the present government in Ottawa to the detriment of western Canada and our city.
We want a place for Manitoba in the transportation sun. We do not intend to rest until we obtain it.

I am not rising to speak, Mr. Chairman, but merely to exercise my right to make a factual correction. I shall have something to say later about some of the points raised in the hon. gentleman's speech. But as a Manitoban perhaps I might be allowed the indulgence of the committee to say I thought the form and the presentation of the hon. member's speech did great credit to my home town.
I am troubled about this one factual question which 1 raised when the hon. member was speaking and I should like to set the record straight. I do not claim to have examined everything which has appeared in the Winnipeg newspapers, but I did see in the Winnipeg Free Press a report which contained, in quotation marks, a statement of mine which went something like this: "I think it is well known that it is the problem of Winnipeg which is holding up the conclusion of the air bilateral." That was in quotation marks. The next sentence was not in quotation marks; it purported to be a paraphrase of what I said. Again, let me point out I am speaking from memory. My memory may not be verbally exact but I am sure of the sense of what I said. I was supposed to have said:	"There will be no bilateral concluded until Winnipeg's demands are satisfied," or something to that effect.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I recall very well the occasion when my statement was made. I said at that time that I did not believe a bilateral agreement would be reached until Winnipeg's claims were met. I said this in the knowledge that we had told the Americans that we were prepared to sign an agreement either if they would give us the right for a Canadian air line to fly from Winnipeg to Chicago, or withdraw their request that an American air line should be permitted to fly between Montreal and Chicago. I believed, as I think nearly every reasonable person would have believed, that they would have chosen to let us have the Winnipeg route, which was, from a monetary standpoint, less interesting, rather than withdraw their request for Montreal-Chicago. But they took the other alternative, something I did not expect them to do. When I expressed 23033-66J

myself in the way I did, I had good reason for that belief. But I never made the categorical statement, and it would have been wrong if I had. I just thought the committee would grant me the indulgence to correct this because I do not like to give wrong impressions.

The minister's standing in the city of Winnipeg is not very high. The fact that he once lived there no longer stands to his credit. However, when other members from Winnipeg were asking questions in the house on January 19-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself-we gained the impression from the minister's answer that nothing can be done until three years have elapsed. This puts the minister in a very peculiar position indeed. I think he will have to go out to Winnipeg to explain it all, and I ask him to do so.
I think I should do that whether I am welcome there or not, but notwithstanding some of the things that have been said I have the impression that I still have a few friends left there.
There are not many Liberals out there.

I must say that I was deeply disappointed that we did not get the Winnipeg-Chicago route, and I want to make another correction. At no time was there any question of a Canadian air line flying the Winnipeg-Minneapolis-Chicago route-it was a direct Winnipeg-Chicago route. The route included in the new bilateral agreement is a direct flight by an American air line from Winnipeg to Minneapolis instead of the very unsatisfactory one that has existed up to now.
What we were trying to get was a direct flight from Winnipeg to Chicago and I think I ought to make that point clear. I am very disappointed we have not got it, but I do think it is very likely, now there is going to be a direct flight from Winnipeg to Minneapolis, that the traffic will grow so rapidly on that route-I share hon. members' hopes in that respect-that there will be no answer to our claim to have the route double-tracked when the question next arises.

speechtext: To some of us in Winnipeg it is pretty important.

I think we should have that flight, but the whole point is that we cannot have an agreement unless both parties say yes. In the end we had to make up our minds or we would go on indefinitely getting no agreement. We had to take what in the judgment of the negotiators was the best we could get at this time. These negotiations were held up for months, and months and months, precisely because of the insistence of the government, and mainly, if it is not immodest of me to say it, of the Minister of Transport, that this Winnipeg question should be settled.

speechtext: You should have held out for another month.

Mr. Chairman, other than a brief sortie into the question period last Friday this also is the first time I have attempted to inflict any words of wisdom on the members of the House of Commons.
As is traditional, I am very tempted to take this opportunity to tell in detail of the many attractions of my riding of Port Arthur and of northwestern Ontario. I am also tempted to try to enlist support for the solution of all the problems of that area, and these are many.
However, I will resist that temptation to cover so much ground until some later date, and will attempt to concentrate on one major field related to the subject under discussion. It seems to me appropriate that, on debate of the Department of Transport estimates, the member for Port Arthur should air his views on a matter of importance, concern and quite extreme emergency to his constituents. I make no apology for the fact that much of what I have to say will be repetitious, some of it already having been mentioned during the course of this debate, but it is sufficiently serious and urgent that I think it bears repetition.
I am referring to the recent alarming developments in one of the most significant fields of transport, the serious dissipation of the

railway passenger services of this country. I feel sure I will be supported in my remarks, at least in principle, by members in all parts of the chamber, and especially by my colleagues from neighbouring constituencies, the hon. member for Fort William and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
All present here, and many throughout the country, are aware of the existence of a fairly comprehensive survey of the railway transportation system of Canada. Like others,
I have had the opportunity to study and review in fair detail the report of the Royal Commission on Transportation. This published survey, known also as the MacPherson report, in volume 1, beginning on page 43, makes very special mention of the problem of passenger services. Essentially the royal commission report appears to contain these observations, to reach these conclusions, and to make certain recommendations.
The key observations are:
"First passenger services are clearly one aspect of rail operation which is uneconomic, taken as a whole."
The second is that the railways have a-
-"continuing need of revenues to cover deficits incurred because of the apparent inability of railway management to slough off the historical, traditional and institutional obligation to provide passenger services."
The third key observation is that the revenue to cover such deficits is-
"a burden which at present must be borne by the users of rail freight services."
The key conclusions of the MacPherson report with regard to passenger services are, first:
Railways must eventually withdraw all uneconomic rail passenger services subject to similar time limitations imposed in connection with the abandonment of uneconomic plant.
And, second:
Immediate and abrupt withdrawal of rail passenger services where they are unprofitable would cause dislocations far outweighing the advantages to be gained.
The key recommendations are that elimination of uneconomic passenger services be proceeded with over a period of five years, and that since those five years could be long enough to have serious consequences for those freight shippers already burdened with high freight rates and the possibility of further increases in freight rates-
-the government of Canada should, in the interests of the nation as a whole, absorb in declining measures-for a period of five years-this most substantial of all obligations now incumbent upon railway management.


And furthermore:
To the extent that there remain after this five year period rail passenger services operating at a loss, but essential because of a lack of alternate surface transportation, it shall be the responsibility of the nation to bear the burden of that loss.
Mr. Chairman, this railway administration, railway efficiency problem, is one of the more complicated and difficult facing the nation internally today.
One cannot argue too much with the validity of the statement that passenger service is uneconomic as a direct return on direct railway investment.
One cannot argue at all about the disadvantages to the economy, and to shippers of freight, inherent in the railways' apparent practice of spreading the passenger service loss over freight rates. Most certainly this is iniquitous to the shippers, and to customers and end-consumers and users of shipped goods.
One cannot really argue with the desire of railway management to operate profitably and, in their eyes, efficiently.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Perhaps in the long term, at some distant future date, the recommended withdrawal from uneconomic passenger service may be the right answer; but even assuming the logic of the eventual withdrawal of such services, which is more than I would care to assume at this stage, there are many considerations of timing, degree and method that must first be resolved before irrevocable action can be taken. There are many interlocking and related problems of both a social and economic nature that must be carefully analysed before even the beginning of this drastic policy of mass abandonment should be condoned or permitted.
In terms of timing, there are areas and regions in this country, which are so sparsely settled with so many isolated communities, where adequate alternative passenger transportation is simply not available and does not yet exist. Let us make no mistake about this that the lack of transportation, including specifically the movement of people, is still a very major economic and social barrier to the development of Canada toward its potential. As is characteristic of so many other aspects, there are vast differences in the transportation needs of the many regions and sub regions of our nation.
A policy such as the elimination of the "Dominion" passenger train by the C.P.R.
Supp ly-Transport
might not be so drastic in the highly developed areas such as the "golden horseshoe" around Toronto or Montreal, but it could be and is most dangerous when applied to areas like northwestern Ontario and western Canada. In these underdeveloped and underpopulated sections our crying need is for more access transportation, not less, and the elimination of passenger train service is not progress to us, but regression. It could cause our regional economy to go backwards, not forward, and for us at the very best this action is very much premature. So timing and degree in a matter like this is vital.
As to method, surely the MacPherson report or the authors thereof did not anticipate or condone even the beginning of implementation of the withdrawal of passenger train services on a national scale before all the related problems could reasonably be analysed and answers worked out; but with the abandonment of the "Dominion", in particular, that withdrawal is being proceeded with at a rapid pace.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, at the pace of abandonment of railway passenger train service by the C.P.R., the discussion or study of railway policy at some future date by this house or by its transportation committee may be academic. The C.P.R. has already eliminated half of its transcontinental train operation, and certainly all the signs point to the dumping of the "Canadian" at the earliest opportunity. If the C.P.R. is permitted to proceed as it is now proceeding, this house and its transportation committee will soon be facing an already accomplished fact, particularly when it attempts to deal with the royal commission on transportation.
To make sure of all this the C.P.R. appears to be embarking on a deliberate policy of not replacing its passenger train capital equipment as it wears out, and in many ways is making its passenger service so expensive, so inconvenient and so unattractive that people will get the message which simply is: Stay away; don't ride with us we don't want you.
The stories of increased fares, of peculiar space reservation tactics, of deteriorating equipment, of frequent delays and so on are being heard on every side, and several of these have been related to some degree in this house by members of all parties. No, there cannot be much doubt that the C.P.R. is jumping the gun and is not waiting for the total study that is so necessary in regard to-this most serious and major matter.


Supply-Transport
By instinct, by training and by experience I lean toward the premise that the government should be very cautious about undue interference with business and private enterprise. By the same token, although the C.P.R. is ostensibly a private enterprise company, it is dealing in a national service and has had very considerable national assistance. Its actions gravely influence the national economy. It is by nature a utility, and this has already been recognized in principle by the Railway Act and by the creation and jurisdiction of the Board of Transport Commissioners. So, more than any other private corporation, it is answerable to the public and to this house.
I suggest that we are entitled to interfere when the national interest is threatened, and it is my opinion, as a result of recent action on the part of the C.P.R., that the national interest is being threatened. Most certainly there is sufficient evidence of public concern to justify our demanding a great deal more information and answers than we have had so far in respect of this railway problem. We have heard no real details from the C.P.R. about its program for the protection of C.P.R. employees who are being or are about to be transferred or displaced, ultimately and potentially by the hundreds. We have heard no suggestions from any source as to what happens to the smaller railway towns and communities such as Schreiber, White River, Kenora and others. What will happen to the small storekeepers, hotel owners and the dozens of other small businessmen who are locked into investments so dependent upon the trade of railway employees who may not be there much longer in many of these towns? Surely this is public business.
We have now experienced in my constituency of Port Arthur, and indeed throughout northwestern Ontario, the fear, the insecurity and the anxiety of so many people who do not know what lies ahead, but who, perhaps with real reason, anticipate the worst. This is not only public business, I consider it to be my very personal business. All these considerations and many more are pertinent to what appears to railway executives to be only a straightforward matter of railway corporate profits or losses.
The performance, profit-wise, of the C.P.R. and C.P.I. and its subsidiaries and associated companies in connection with its responsibility to its shareholders, has not been bad.
The continuation of passenger service will not in the immediate future threaten the C.P.R.'s corporate existence, particularly if a
[Mr. Andras.l
reasonable compromise solution is worked out in the near future in terms of the nation absorbing some of the passenger losses so that freight services do not subsidize passenger service. Surely the C.P.R. can be reasonably expected to be patient. This is not so simple a problem that it can be dealt with as just one of immediate corporate profits or losses. This requires study, and the time to study it thoroughly.
The appeal of the ruling of the Board of Transport Commissioners, allowing the C.P.R. abandonment of the "Dominion", will be heard by the cabinet soon. Incidentally it seems peculiar, to say the least that in spite of the knowledge of this pending appeal the transport board the day before yesterday proceeded to let the C.P.R. eliminate even the summer run of the "Dominion".
It has also been suggested that the transportation committee of this house should sit down with C.P.R. management to get a clear-cut picture of their forward plans regarding passenger train service.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Surely until this has been done and until the MacPherson report has been fully aired and dealt with, together with all the related problems, and until a consensus of this nation has been formally reached and identified, it is reasonable to ask that the C.P.R. should itself delay any further dissipation of its passenger service and indeed even reverse its decision regarding the "Dominion".
In the absence of this voluntary action by the C.P.R., which I realize we might be extremely naive to expect, I can assure the government that a decision by it, if necessary through this house, to disallow the Board of Transport Commissioners ruling regarding the "Dominion" would be extremely well received in the Port Arthur riding and, I suggest, throughout all of western Canada.
With this type of moratorium it would then be possible to deal rationally and objectively with the whole railway program and its interlocking relationship with all segments of our nation and its people, through the house transportation committee and then the house itself, in full consultation with railway management and the railway unions. Failing that, Mr. Chairman, I anticipate-if I judge the mood of the people correctly-that the C.P.R. will face the toughest and most militant union resistance in its long history during the next contract negotiations.

I further anticipate that the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Transportation will, when they are dealt with, find many of the members of this house from all parties and the people of Canada in a pretty ugly mood, beamed particularly toward the Canadian Pacific Railway.
After all, the people of this country through huge grants of land and money gave this company its start and provided it with many assets that have always been highly profitable.
The C.P.R. has an obligation to this nation, and through the medium of this house and its attendant publicity I call upon this company to recognize and honour that debt by showing a great deal more patience and national responsibility, or alternatively perhaps this debt should be paid by returning to the people in full current measure those original grants.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to avail myself this evening of the opportunity to make a few remarks in the debate on the estimates of the Department of Transport. I only regret that I did not have this opportunity six months ago. Of course, we would have had that opportunity had not the Prime Minister of this country decided that an election was more important than carrying on the nation's business. As a result, in the intervening time many problems that existed six months ago have multiplied. I believe this is why we are having a rather exciting debate on the minister's estimates at the present time.
I have been concerned since coming back to this house in 1963 with the policy of the present government with respect to transport. It seems to me it is a rather will-o'-the-wisp, musical chairs, now you see it, now you don't, sort of policy. Those remarks are not made frivolously, Mr, Chairman. To back up what I have said may I refer specifically to what I believe to be one of the most serious problems facing Canada today. I refer to the railway line abandonment problem which has been hanging fire for four or five years, ever since the MacPherson report was brought in.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the former government under the right hon. Leader of the Opposition had a very comprehensive bill ready to present to the house when the present government took over. That bill was apparently scrapped and thrown into the wastepaper basket, and another policy was instituted. The interesting thing is that the
Supply-Transport
present Minister of Public Works was then the Minister of Transport. I do not know whether he found this problem too hot a potato but he immediately threw it into the lap of the Minister of Agriculture. I had the privilege of speaking in 1964 on the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture because at that time, as I say, it was his responsibility. Then apparently the Minister of Agriculture also decided that it was too hot a potato for him and he threw it back into the hands of the present Minister of Transport.
The Minister of Transport then turned it over to his efficient officials-I must say they are efficient in this department-and apparently left the matter entirely in their hands, because it seems they called in Mr. Donald Gordon and Mr. Crump, the top officials of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., and as a result Bill No. C-120 was presented to the house. Everybody knows what happened to that bill. After 12 or 15 meetings of the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines this bill, too, was scrapped and thrown into the wastepaper basket. Today we are back where we were, and this heavy cloud of uncertainty and doubt is still hanging over western Canada.
My remarks this evening are not directed to rail line abandonment, Mr. Chairman, because I know the government has another bill ready to present to the house and I shall have an opportunity to make some remarks on that bill at a later time. I just mention the problem of rail line abandonment to illustrate that we have cause for concern in western Canada as far as transport is concerned.
I want to be one of the first to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg South upon the very comprehensive and lucid contribution he made to the debate this evening.
Hear, hear.

He also pointed out some of the will-o'-the-wisp problems that we have out in western Canada. We have a problem as far as air transport is concerned. This problem affects that great city of Winnipeg, the gateway to the west, Saskatoon, Regina, Moose Jaw and other points in western Canada. In addition to these problems we have those of run-throughs, master agencies, railway station abandonment and the depletion of railway passenger service, a recent example of which was the withdrawal of the "Dominion". I am sure we shall hear more about that.
Then last but not least, Mr. Chairman, is the problem of shortage of box cars. We


Supp ly-Transport
heard a very good, comprehensive contribution on this subject yesterday afternoon from the hon. member for Lethbridge who led off in this debate. I was very interested, also, in the contributions made by various members on the other side of the chamber with regard to the problem of box car shortage. Yesterday the Minister of Finance, under whose jurisdiction lies the Canadian Wheat Board, made the brave statement that now approximately 600 box cars a day are being utilized in the movement of grain. However, Mr. Chairman, the facts do not bear out the minister's statement, because as the hon. member for Lethbridge pointed out there are figures which indicate there is still a serious problem in this area. I wish to re-emphasize those figures.
I have here the latest report of the Canadian Wheat Board with regard to quota distribution as at February 7, 1966. This statement gives comparative figures for 1964-65 and 1965-66. In February, 1964, there were no points in Saskatchewan on a two-bushel quota; at the present time we have 48 points on a two-bushel quota. In 1964-65 there were 14 points on a three-bushel quota in Saskatchewan, and at the present time we have 157 such points. In 1964-65 we had 327 points on a five-bushel quota; this year we have 260. In 1964-65 we had 475 points on a six-bushel quota, and at the present time we have only 230; in other words, in 1964-65 about twice as many points were on higher quota. These are alarming facts as they affect the western farmer.
There is a contradiction in this situation. The Minister of Finance told us yesterday how wonderful the situation is and what an acceleration there has been in the removal of grain in box cars. Yet under the date of January 20 we see this headline in the Ottawa Citizen, "Box-car pile-up clash in making with C.P.R. head". The article reads in part:
Agriculture Minister Greene, whose colleagues now call him "Choo Choo" Greene after his slashing attacks on the C.P.R., has found that there are 21,000 Canadian box cars now tied up from Winnipeg to Chicago.
The article says later:
This, he argues, is 5,000 more box cars out of the country at this critical time than in any other January since 1962. In the years between 1962 and 1965, the average number of box cars at loose in the U.S. only totalled between 15,000 and 16,000.
And this at a time when the total number of box cars in Canada was 5,500 less than four years ago. Right now the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. each have a total of 10,000 each at work in this country.

[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
This, of course, illustrates the difference of opinion between the ministries with regard to the box car shortage. This evening, I want to deal with one particular facet of this box car shortage. The minister will recall that on January 21, after the house opened, I put a question to him relating to this problem. He admitted that there was a problem. I think the reason he did this was that last July I had the opportunity and good fortune of getting a little information about this subject. It so happened that a railwayman from the United States, the New York Central Railway, who asked me not to divulge his name, was spending a holiday in Canada following his retirement. We were discussing the relative problems of agriculture in the United States and Canada and our conversation moved around to the utilization of box cars in the United States. He said he was immeasurably surprised at the increase in the usage of Canadian box cars in the United States over the last three or four years.
I proceeded to ask him his opinion as to the reason for this increase. He made several observations and I think the house and the minister would be interested in them. He said that it seemed our Canadian railroads had a better maintenance scheme for box cars than they had in the United States. As a result when our cars were sent down to the United States with the large volume of Canadian products, such as paper, wood pulp and so on, under the reciprocal agreement the United States railroads loved to have the opportunity to utilize those box cars as long as they could.
Now, we have the deterrent of the per diem demurrage or the return charge for these cars. I am going to put some figures on the record in a few minutes which will emphasize the point I am trying to make. He went on to say, too, that he felt the recent devaluation of the dollar in Canada worked to the advantage of United States railroads because apparently there has been no increase in demurrage charges in the last few years to offset the economic advantage the United States railroads have of approximately 8 per cent in a decrease the demurrage charges.
We find this situation has developed and has amplified in the last few years. Another basic problem is the fact that the economies of both the United States and Canada have become increasingly more buoyant over the last few years and the gross national product


has been going up. There has been more interchange between the two countries, and we are glad of that fact. In looking over the statistics, I find that the railroads in Canada have not kept pace with this increased economic growth by adding new cars. Here again, I think the railroads are at fault. There are a number of factors that contribute to the shortage, but here is a basic one. Possibly our railroads have not been as optimistic as this government and former governments about the increase in our exports, particularly grain, with the result that possibly they are following the philosophy that automation will permit them to keep up to the demand that is made on transportation facilities with the same number of cars.
Apparently this judgment is in error because we find now that we have one of the greatest shortages of box cars in the history of western Canada or, in fact, in Canadian history. I should like to substantiate one of these remarks of mine by a letter I have received through the minister's department. After I had this conversation with this United States railroad official, I took the matter up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time and the Minister of Transport. They were very courteous and made an investigation into it. Apparently they took up the question with the Canadian National, and I do not know if they got any reply from the Canadian Pacific. Mr. Arbique, the secretary to Mr. Vaughan of Canadian National, has written a letter and I should like to put a portion of it on the record. This letter is dated August 30, 1965 and reads in part as follows:
The return of Canadian box cars from the United States and the United States box cars from Canada is governed by rules of the Association of American Railroads which permits use of the cars to or in the direction of the car owners. The United States customs regulations do not permit the use of Canadian cars in U.S. domestic service except in accordance with the above rules.
Here is the salient point of the letter in the last line:
Regardless of this, some of the Canadian cars are no doubt used in contravention of the rules.
This, Mr. Chairman, is what is actually occurring. There is an excessive use of our cars in the United States in contravention of the rules. As I mentioned a while ago, possibly one of the reasons is that our demurrage charges have not been increased. To emphasize this point I cite a headline in the Western Producer, which reads:	"Boxcar
Supply-Transport
situation draws fire at annual meeting of C.F.A." I have already given the quotation on the box car ball-up, as it was referred to by the Minister of Agriculture, but in order to be a little more specific I should like to give some statistics with regard to the use of box cars and the number of box cars we have in use in Canada, as well as those in the United States.
These figures come from a report of the Railway Association of Canada to the Board of Transport Commissioners of Canada, and I am giving a three year summary. I took a three year summary in order to be fair. This is a three year summary of Canadian and United States railway box car locations. On December 18, 1963, Canadian box cars in the United States totalled 19,035. This was at that particular date, and approximately the same cut-off date is used for each year. United States box cars in Canada totalled 7,734. Now, compare those figures, 19,035 and 7,734. On December 22, 1964 Canadian box cars in the United States totalled 20,246, while United States box cars in Canada numbered 7,267. Even with the increasing buoyancy of our economy we see the figures developing in favour of the United States. On December 17, 1965, Canadian box cars in the United States totalled 21,031, while United States box cars in Canada numbered 7,591. So, between 1963 and 1965 we find an increase of over 2,000 more Canadian box cars down in the United States. This substantiates the attitude taken by the Minister of Agriculture toward the Canadian Pacific, although he quoted 5,000.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
These figures do not quite bear out the figures used by the minister. I should like to quote from a summary of the total cars owned by Canadian railways, which gives the complete total of all types of cars, that is box cars, refrigerator cars, gondola, open top and hopper type, covered hopper, stock, flat and others. This is the total for three years, and I find that on December 18, 1963, the total number of cars in Canada was 173,950. This is the total number of cars owned by all railroads in Canada. The total number of box cars was 104,091, and if you compare the figure 173,950 with the 104,091, you can see the percentage of box cars to the total. We are talking about box cars, which are by far the most important and basic part of the problem.
On December 22, 1964 the total number of box cars was 172,089 showing a decrease of


Supply-Transport
about 1,100 cars, which is quite a drop. The total number of cars as of December 22, 1964 was 102,571.
On December 17, 1965, the most recent figures available, the total number of cars in use in Canada was 173,883, and the total number of box cars was 102,077. Compared with the total number of box cars on December 17, 1965, of 102,077, you will see quite a depletion, over 2,000 cars, compared with the total on December 18, 1963 of 104,091. This bears out my statement a few minutes ago that both railroads have missed the boat when it comes to analysing the buoyancy of the economy and the necessity for box cars to supply our commercial needs. There should be an increase rather than a decrease.
I should like to refer to the official railway equipment register, which is rather interesting. This is a code of per diem rules for freight, commonly referred to as demurrage charges. This is an agreed settlement for the use of railroad-owned freight cars between common carrier railroads in Canada and the United States.
In other words these are penalty charges as they affect our cars going to the United States or United States cars coming into Canada. These per diem rates are arrived at on the original cost of railway box cars depreciated, and I should like to use one of the tables to illustrate my point.
These demurrage charges are, interestingly enough, based on the depreciated value of the box cars. This is what the present value is. A box car which has depreciated $1,000 or less carries a demurrage charge of $2.16 per day. From $1,000.01 to $5,000.01 the charge is $2.79 per day. From $5,000.01 to $10,000, which is group 3 the charge is $3.88 per day. From $10,000.01 to $15,000 the charge is $4.50 per day. From $15,000.01 to $20,000 the charge is $6.15. From $20,000.01 to $25,000 it is $7.11 per day. From $25,000.01 to $30,000 it is $9.00 per day. From $30,000.01 to $35,000 the charge is $10.18; and from $35,000.01 and over, which is a rare group because there are not many box cars in that class, the charge is $12.18 per day. The interesting fact here is that most of our cars used for handling grain fall between category 4 and category 7; so in other words, the charge is between $4.50 and $9.00 per day.
That may sound like quite a bit of money. But supposing we have several thousand box cars which have gone across the line and there is a particular need for a good car. We

have found that there has been a tendency on the part of our United States friends to utilize our best cars, and we need our best cars for moving grain. In view of the freight rates in the United States as compared with Canadian rates, it favours the United States to use our cars for 30 days or so on inter-state commerce, rather than direct them back to Canada. Why should they worry about paying a small demurrage charge of from $4.50 to $9.00 a day if they can make $400 or $500 on carrying freight with one car? You can see, Mr. Chairman, how these discrepancies creep in. This type of situation should be investigated in relation to extended use of our box cars.
The reciprocal agreement specifically states that as soon as a car carrying our produce, such as pulpwood or paper, which is one of our biggest exports, is sent to its destination, it should be loaded with United States exports and directed back to the point from whence it came.
If this agreement were lived up to we would not have so much of a problem as we do have. However, information which I got from the U.S.A. railroader who had been on the New York Central for 40 years was to the contrary. He told me they are not living up to the agreement down in the States and he did not blame us for being disturbed about it. I suggest this modest demurrage sum is not a big enough deterrent. This matter should be looked into in order to alleviate some of our problems.
I think this pretty well points up the problem of excessive use of box cars in the United States. I could go on at some length and put some additional facts on the record, but I think what I have said will suffice.
I should like to mention in passing another matter which has exercised us in western Canada recently. This is the suggestion that the St. Lawrence tolls be increased. I am not going to deal with this but I do want to say this for the record in passing.
The Canadian wheat producers see higher seaway tolls as a direct charge against the farmers' take home pay. Mr. Charles W. Gibbings, president of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers and the Saskatchewan Wheat Pools made these views known as spokesman for 160,000 prairie farmers in a brief presented to the Seaway Authority recently.
As I say, this is a matter of deep concern to western Canadians and I hope that the minister, when he is formulating his policy on this


question, will take this into consideration as well as what I have said with reference to the shortage of box cars, with particular emphasis on this excessive use in the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on item 1 of the minister's estimates to discuss some matters about Vancouver Quadra, and about the port of Vancouver. I am sorry if in the course of doing so anything that I say here this evening in any way shortens the very valuable remarks which I know my hon. and valued friend, the hon. member for York-Humber might make in the continuation of his romp through the sewers in Montreal which intrigued us the other evening. I am sorry that I am perhaps not able to bring any such lurid terms to the house.
I want to speak of the port of Vancouver. There are some points I wish to talk about which I believe are as important as those my hon. friend raised in respect of the water levels of the Great Lakes, and the St. Lawrence.
Mr. Chairman, one day in going through the maritime museum in Vancouver I came upon some descriptive panels describing the growth and development of the port of Vancouver, and they had this to say in introducing the subject:
A port controlled by the National Harbours Board but with 60 per cent of its facilities owned by other interests.
A shipbuilding port where few ships are built.
It is unfortunate that the Minister of Industry is not in the house this evening, as it is a subject which I am sure he would appreciate and understand.
A port with old docks for new liners.
I will talk about that a little later.
A port almost unknown to the city around it.
A port in a metro area with three separate port authorities.
A port with overlapping and often conflicting land tenures.
A port governed and administered by many
bodies.


Supply-Transport
The port, sir, is quite an important one.
I have here a paper brought out in 1964 on the port of Vancouver, by the National Harbours Board describing that port, in which it says that it has the largest dry cargo dock on the west coast of the Americas and, moreover, that it handles 26 per cent of Canada's export trade.
Yet, despite the contribution which the port of Vancouver makes to the economy of Canada, this port has consistently received less consideration on any basis of measurement than the other great eastern port, namely Montreal.
To make some basis of comparison I took the capital investment which has been placed into these two great ports by the National Harbours Board over the years since the end of the war. I set these two on an index figure based on 1949. In 1949 the fixed assets of the port of Montreal, as set out by the National Harbours Board, and these were National Harbours Board assets, were $67.7 million. That is exclusive of the assets of the bridges. In the same year, 1949, the fixed assets of Vancouver were $25.1 million. I took these two figures and set those in 1949, as an index number of 100.
By the time we come along to 1963, being the last year for which I took figures, the port of Montreal fixed assets had expanded to $145.6 million, and the fixed assets of Vancouver had expanded to $41.4 million. If you look at the index, the index of fixed assets for Montreal have increased from 100 in 1949 to 217 in 1963, which is a little more than double. The assets for Vancouver have increased from 100 in 1949 to 165 in 1963.
Let me put it another way. What it means is that over the years, year in and year out, from one government to another, the port of Montreal has received one third more than the port of Vancouver in investment in it, on any basis that you want to examine.
I want to discuss a little bit about the effect of the retardation of capital development by the National Harbours Board over these years since its formation in 1936, and what that has done to the port of Vancouver. Before I go into that for a moment let me preface my remarks by explaining to the house one of the slight differences between the port of Montreal and the port of Vancouver.
In 1936 when the National Harbours Board took over, it took over from the old Harbour Commission of Montreal virtually a whole harbour and with it the administration of the whole harbour.

In the case of the port of Vancouver, however, about one third of the port of Vancouver was at that time operated and owned by the National Harbours Board, the balance being operated by private enterprise, which at that time and even today is to a great extent in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Let us take a look at how this development has gone on, and what the effect has been upon the development of the city of Vancouver's great port. If we look at that portion of land stretching to the entrance of Stanley park, which many members of the house well know, and look eastward toward the heart of the city, toward Burrard street and the foot of Granville street, one will see the great area of the Canadian Pacific Railway holdings. This is the area which has been in dispute between the federal government and the Canadian Pacific Railway since the Canadian Pacific first went into that area. It is a dispute which has been negotiated, and has been under negotiation between the National Harbours Board and the Canadian Pacific since 1931.
While the moneys received from rent in that area have been placed into an escrow account, the result is that in that area you can go down and find that it is a jungle of crumbling boatworks, the reason being that no one wants to put any investment into an area which is entirely under dispute, in which no long term arrangements can be made, and in which no satisfactory explanation can be given as to who is the owner of property. As you move along this valuable harbour land it is simply little more than a harbour slum.
I want to quote to the house a line or two from the Vancouver Sun of February 13, 1964, when that newspaper wrote a feature story on the subject. The heading of it is: "Waterfront of Vancouver Stunted by Birth Defect". It tells about this long dispute between the Canadian Pacific and the National Harbours Board. A portion of it reads as follows:
Ownership of these water lots has never been agreed on by Canadian Pacific Railways and National Harbours Board. Rentals are thrown into a trust account, pending settlement.
A little later it says:
The Harbours Board has contested C.P.R. ownership of the water lots from Gore to Cardero.
For legal reasons, the principle is being fought on the Cardero-Burrard section. A decision, if ever reached, will be applied to the entire section.


A Harbours Board spokesman said Wednesday the dispute has been going on since the 1930's.
Rentals estimated in the millions are held in escrow.
The disputant parties have negotiated periodically, but the Harbours Board official said the dispute likely will have to go to the Exchequer Court.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I hope the minister when he visits Vancouver will be able to announce that he has reached some agreement with the C.P.R. with respect to this property so that we shall know who the owners are, either the C.P.R. or the National Harbours Board. Then those who want to do business upon this wharf can put some investment into it with some assurance as to who their landlord is and with some hope for future development in the area. I understand this question is again being taken up between the Harbours Board and the C.P.R. But this has been going on for more than 30 years and my plea to the minister is: For God's sake get on with it, get this settled and let Vancouver people have the use of this enormously valuable piece of waterfront.

This was taken as a personal insult by Mr. R. A. Emerson, company president, and he called a press conference in Winnipeg to refute the charges and put the blame on the port facilities.
Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp, who is answerable to parliament for the Canadian Wheat Board, backed up these charges and this brought a quick reaction from the Vancouver Merchants Exchange.

The facts are that there are nine terminals at the Pacific coast, including six at Vancouver, with a capacity of almost 25 million bushels, and as of last Monday-
This was January 29.
-there were only about 12 million bushels of grain and oil seeds in storage-far below working capacity.
To meet the heavy sales commitments out of Pacific ports this winter, a daily unload of about 550 cars is required, and the average daily unloads for the month of January were 395 cars.
This has put exporters in an untenable position. Although there were 21 vessels in port to load grain and oil seeds, only eight were on berth and the other 13 were anchored in the harbour piling up demurrage charges.
One of these vessels is expected to load 45,000 tons and another 35,000 tons, almost 3 million bushels of wheat, and two other vessels of over 25,000 tons each are expected in port shortly to lift grain.
Thus the facts do not bear out Mr. Emerson's laments.
Perhaps this is a good time to mention that the transportation slowdown has affected other grains as well as wheat. Rape seed in particular is in short supply at the Pacific coast and exporters are having difficulty in filling their orders. It is, of course, true that the facilities at the port of Vancouver have not been developed sufficiently to handle all the business that could be directed their way. Unfortunately they have not been getting the grain they could handle which is the fact that the Board of Trade in Vancouver and the port authorities have been trying to emphasize. And this is the central concern of all the farmers.
I would like to make a few comments too on the provisions of the suggested bill in relation to rail line abandonments. I hope that the minister will see that the rationalization authority is given more power than it had in Bill C-120. It must not be left with the sole duty of setting a day for the abandonment. It should be given power to stop an abandonment completely where the social factors to the people concerned warrant it. I think it most unwise, too, that the Board of Transport Commissioners should have no recourse but to accept the figures presented by the railway. Surely independent investigations by competent accountants should be made. I hope that the minister will accept these suggestions in the spirit in which they are made, for we would like to see a railway bill which is fair to all of Canada.
The western Canadian sees the Great Lakes waterway as his doorway to the sea. For decades almost all the grain went through


that doorway. He views with suspicion any attempts to restrict the traffic which flows through it. It is easy to understand then why he dislikes the tolls which are charged. Recently the president of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association, as reported in the Manitoba Co-Operator of January 27, scored the seaway tolls as harming our economy. I should like to quote from that article:
The president and general manager of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association has suggested that the Canadian government has adopted a double standard for the nation's exports.
Stuart Armour of Toronto, addressing the Winnipeg Lions Club last week, said the federal government on one hand is constantly urging Canadians to increase their volume of exports. Yet on the other hand, the federal government had established an "inconsistent and discriminatory" policy of St. Lawrence Seaway tolls which worsened the competitive position of Canadian produce in overseas markets.
I emphasize the last part of that sentence. We would like to see seaway tolls removed completely. We know that by imposing the tolls it was intended to recover the $313 million that Canada put into building her part of the seaway from Montreal to lake Ontario. But we believe that it would be better for Canada to go back to her traditional waterways policy of no tolls. If the waterway is used to the full the increase in productivity in the nation and the savings to the nation would enable us to carry these costs. Now Ottawa is setting about improving the Welland canal and expects to spend something like $374 million when we consider the complete expense involved. It is true that the tolls on the Welland canal were suspended in 1962 and re-suspended again in 1964. If this could be done in these years it can be done permanently. There is some question as to whether the improving and twinning of the Welland canal is the right solution at this point in the river.
The canal then would only be able to take a ship carrying 26,000 tons. Perhaps it would be better to consider the Welland canal as obsolete in this present day to large ships and build a new one which could accommodate
50,000	tonners.
Of course, we all know that the level of the tolls on the international sections of the waterways are a matter of agreement between the United States and Canada, so that we can do little about that. But I do think that we should constantly strive to keep these tolls at as low a level as possible, as well as eliminat-
Supply-Transport
ing them completely if at all possible. Certainly we can do this in our own section of the waterway.
I believe I cannot do better than end this section with a quote from the same article in the Manitoba Co-Operator which gives the words of Mr. Armour:
"Let me assure you that your dependence, as well as that of all other Canadians, on the St. Lawrence waterway and the Canadian railways which serve it, for the level of your business activity and the degree of prosperity you enjoy, is greater today than it ever was", the speaker concluded.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I close by saying a few words about the television problem in my constituency.
Channel 13?

There is no channel 13 in my constituency. There is only one channel. The other day the hon. member for Saskatoon asked the minister what is being done about a C.B.C. outlet for Saskatoon. This has been in the works now for something like three years and we are still waiting to see what is going to happen.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Of course we are much interested in this proposition, and hope that the minister will use his good offices to see that the C.B.C. starts a station in that particular area. We understand that if this is done the present station in Saskatoon, CFQC-TV will join the C.T.V. network. This would take the satellite at Stranraer off the C.B.C. network and put it in the C.T.V. network. We know that Swift Current television would like to put a satellite in the Kindersley constituency. Since this station is a C.B.C. station this would give a large part of the constituency two channels where now there is one.
Toronto may have 13 but we are limited to one. We would like to get another. Much of my constituency, in fact most of it, is in what is known as a remote area. I am sure that the minister understands what their attitude is to large sums being spent on colour television when they have imperfect reception for only one channel. The addition of another channel might prepare them to accept with better grace the huge sums which the C.B.C. intends to spend on colour television. I would ask the minister if he would then urge the C.B.C. to open a station at Saskatoon.

Hear, hear.
