Mr. Chairman, I should like this evening to complete the remarks I started yesterday afternoon. Before returning directly to the St. Lawrence channel at the Cornwall dam, which is the point I had reached yesterday when we were cut over to channel 3 of the Department of Transport, I should like to make a correction in the Hansard report of my remarks of yesterday afternoon. On page 975, I am reported to have said:
To allow the level of Lake Ontario to go below
244.78	feet while relying on the prayers of cabinet ministers and the laws of heaven to refill the basin is a shocking basis on which to operate.
What I said was: "to rely on the prayers of a cabinet minister and the rains of heaven to refill the basin is a shocking basis on which to operate."
In my remarks as of yesterday afternoon I pointed out that the sewage situation in Montreal was the main cause of the low water levels of Lake Ontario, because of the demands of the people in that area that a 35 foot water depth be maintained in Montreal harbour. I recited the priority table in the international agreement between the United States and Canada pointing out that the first use of water, as agreed upon between the United States and Canada, was for health and sanitation purposes, second, for navigation and third, power. I pointed out that the navigation interests of Montreal were being given priority over the first item on the table, and second, that the power interests in the third position were being given privileges that were not theirs under the treaty.
Since I spoke yesterday and before I reach my conclusion, I have been called by some radio stations in Montreal wanting to know what my objection was to the Montreal sewage system. I said I have not the slightest objection to their doing what they want with the sewage of Montreal but please leave the level of Lake Ontario at the minimum of
244.78	feet.
I had a member of the house refer to my comments, and I can only say in that regard that the cricket sings a very nice song, and I guess that it is considered very aesthetic because of its singing, but the advice given to the cricket has been: Go to the ant thou cricket, consider her ways and be wise. We may not have the great civilization as shown in the great art galleries and musical centres of Montreal, but we have taken the ant as our example in Ontario and we have placed

the basic tenets of civilization first. We cannot imagine a person enjoying singing while standing in sewage. We prefer to clear up the sewage situation and then set to singing. But we could be wrong.
In complimenting the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the action he has taken quietly and efficiently during the past year, during which time numerous speakers have referred to the low level of Lake Ontario, I should say that we were very happy to find the water level in Toronto harbour at 244.02 feet, on February 3, which is an improvement of 2.7 feet in one year. I must emphasize that this improvement of 2.7 feet in one year still leaves the water level in Toronto harbour 9.1 inches below the 94 year average.
What is the use of the dams at Cornwall and Iroquois to control the water level of Lake Ontario if, with the two dams in position, right now in the first week of 1966, the water level of Lake Ontario is 9.1 inches below the 94 year average. We had better treatment under the laws of nature for 94 years than we get from our manually controlled dams at Cornwall and Iroquois.
I would emphasize to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that while we appreciate all that he has done during the past year, the people residing in the basin of Lake Ontario-and I emphasize the basin of Lake Ontario, because the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself lives in the basin of Lake St. Clair-are as separated from the other five great lakes as though there were no connection between them whatsoever.
Lake Superior has been controlled for 40 years. That is not so when it comes to controlling the water level of Lake Ontario. The water level of Lake Superior has been controlled within a variation of 18 inches for 40 years, because of the dam work at Sault Ste. Marie, under the authority of the International Joint Commission established in the 1920's.
The level of the water in Lake Ontario could be controlled within such a narrow margin also, if there is no interference with the operation of the control dams.
The power authorities, by which I mean Ontario Hydro and the New York State Power Authority, are only too pleased to let the water go through the dams at Cornwall in order to maintain the 35 foot depth at Montreal. What better argument could they use than: "We are maintaining the water level in Montreal harbour. The people downstream are screaming." They do not say that


they are developing power left, right and centre.
That power blackout we had in the month of November, the day after the election-how many of you realize that Canada suffered a great blackout on the day after the November 8 election-was written up. I would draw to your attention a report-
A blackout on this side?

I am speaking of your side too, my friend. On page 26 of Newsweek magazine for 29 November, 1965, they have a heading: "What Went Wrong?" referring to the blackout in the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. They have a very interesting statement. Newsweek denies that it has any editorial policies, so I have called it a statement, since it appears in a news story.
-the basic trouble is the power generating shortage of the Toronto area.
This, of course, shows that the demand for power at the moment is greater than our generating capacity. Then Newsweek says:
The Federal Power Commission is expected to accent two lessons of the blackout in its report this week: 1. There is no substitute for adequate power generation. 2. More imagination must be used to protect entire systems from local faults.
I should like to point out to the house that Newsweek is putting the cart before the horse in these two statements. The basic trouble is not a power generating shortage in the Toronto area. The basic trouble is overloading transmission lines built for a certain amount of power, and when an extra surge of power is put on, it blows out the control panels.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Then it continues:
The Federal Power Commission is expected to accent two lessons of the blackout in its report this week: (1) There is no substitute for adequate power generation. (2) More imagination must be used to protect entire systems from local faults.
Why not cut down the use to which the power can be put and thus cut our coats according to our cloth? There is no reason why electric power should be generated in Cornwall to be used in illuminating the window fronts of stores and used car lots, to operate electric razors, hair dryers and all kinds of things we did not have 20 years ago. In generating enough power to meet the demand we are affecting the level of lake Ontario despite the fact that electric power is in third position when it comes to priorities, and public health is in first position.
Supply-Transport
I say to the minister that he should establish a basic level for Lake Ontario.-set the average level of 244.78 feet as the base level and let the power development people on the St. Lawrence start from that point up to the high level point of the last few years, something up to 247 feet. There should be ancillary power sources at Cornwall provided by steam or atomic power generation. When the water level had fallen to 244.78 feet, let the power needs of the area be met by power ancillary to hydro. But do not drain Lake Ontario dry so as to flush the sewage of Montreal to the sea. If Montreal does not wish to spend its money on an effective sewer system, as is the practice in all other parts of the civilized world, I would ask them to open the dams that Quebec hydro owns on the Ottawa river and take their flushing water from there. But they are not anxious to take their flushing water from the Ottawa river. They know that Quebec has too many hydro installations there. Do they want to flush their sewage to the open sea? Well, for the benefit of the people who will be attending the great expose of 1967 let them take water from the Ottawa river and let us enjoy the waters of Ontario at a minimum level of 244.78.
I have in my hand a copy of the Family Herald dated April 15, 1965. In this article Mr. J. S. Cram writes:
Here Montreal interests come into sharp conflict with those of cities higher up the waterway. If Montreal got more water out of the amount in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence system, the others would be left with less... These sharers of the common waterway are not small fry, and their interests are not confined to Ontario and Quebec. Besides our own cities such as Windsor, Hamilton and Toronto there are several important U.S. lake ports such as Milwaukee, Buffalo, Cleveland, Detroit and Chicago. Among them these cities alone have 71 million people who have just as much need for water as have Montrealers.
I would draw the attention of the Minister of Transport and of the Secretary of State for External Affairs particularly to the next sentence in this article written by Mr. Cram:
Not susceptible to the sort of political treatment that works in Canada, the U.S. centres will make sure that their interests are protected in any agreement that is drawn up.
"Not susceptible to the sort of political treatment that works in Canada-" I do not understand what that means. The minister might explain, perhaps, what Mr. Cram meant when he wrote that phrase.
I wish, now, to refer to a subject I have been trying to cover in the last few months


Supply-Transport
by means of questions or by raising the subject on what we call "the late show".
As I stated the other day it is ridiculous to try to cover the situation in such a manner. It has to do with another item concerning navigation-one which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport and of the Secretary of State for External Aflairs. I am referring to the so-called patented waterlots in lake Ontario and in particular to those on the lake Ontario shore of York-Humber and York West between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek.
Now just about 11 months ago, as hon. members wih find in their Hansards at page 12689, I directed a question on the subject to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Under the heading of "Public Works, Long Branch, Ontario; dumping of fill into Lake Ontario" I asked the following question on the orders of the day:
I have a question I should like to direct to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the International Joint Commission given authority to anyone to dump fill into Lake Ontario between the mouth of the Humber Hiver and the mouth of Etobicoke Creek, thus affecting the water levels of this international body of water?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will see that this important matter is looked into.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Do the owners of so-called water lots lying south of Mimico and Long Branch, on Lake Ontario, enjoy an immunity from the regulations of the International Joint Commission?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure that because of the technical aspects involved in the question I would not be expected to give an immediate response, but I will look into it.
That is the end of the chapter. That is the end of the lesson. That is the end of the inquiry. Nothing has ever been said about the subject by the Secretary of State for External Affairs from that day to this. Now when I stand up and ask whether this illegal fill at Long Branch has been approved by the Secretary of State for External Affairs or by the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Justice tells me this fill does not interfere with navigation and that his department has, therefore, taken no interest in the matter, despite the fact that this constitutes a violation of the International Boundary Waters Treaty.
I would draw attention to the fact that I have in my hand a political pamphlet put out by the New Democratic candidate in York West, a fine girl, Martha Brewin, who ran against the successful candidate, Hon. Robert Winters. It is a nice little pamphlet. She does
(Mr. Cowan.]
not live in the riding so in an effort to curry favour with the voters a publicity agent took her around and had photographs of her taken at various places in the riding.
One of the most interesting pictures, to my mind, showed her standing on this fill jutting out into lake Ontario for 470 feet with a width of 330 feet-this development which, the Minister of Justice says, is no problem to navigation. What does the caption under the picture say?
Martha Brewin, N.D.P. candidate in West York, is familiarizing herself with all the local problems of the riding. Here she is standing on the illegal fill at Long Branch.
I presume from this pamphlet that had she been successful in gaining a majority she would be helping me in bringing the cabinet to the point at which it would enforce the act which prohibits the dumping of fill in international boundary waters without prior consent.
Did you try to help her win?

Mr. Winters promised to help, too.
They tell me this is not an obstruction to navigation. I have in my hands some clippings from the New Toronto Advertiser, a weekly paper printed in the riding of West York and circulating in Mimico which is in the riding of York-Humber. It is pointed out that on this piece of land, which is no obstacle to navigation, they want to erect two 18 storey towers containing 500 suites. This is the new proposal. Anyone can understand how ephemeral a piece of land is when a proposal is made to place two huge buildings on it. The Minister of Justice says it is no obstacle to navigation. Yet the Minister of Public Works writes saying:
Our engineers recommend that lights be installed at the outer ends of the filled areas .... throughout the navigation season.
Why would he write that way when the Minister of Justice says this constitutes no obstruction to navigation? I do not know.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
However, in this newspaper story we read:
James McCallum, lawyer appearing for the developers, said that the original plan which called for a hotel had been changed because it was not economically possible to run a hotel in this location.
One questions how they could build hotels easily in Lake Ontario without interfering with navigation, but Mr. McCallum went on to say:
All hotels and motor hotels now-a-days have to be in the hands of a management organization. No


mortgages are granted unless you are under some big chain.
McCallum, speaking of the density factor with regard to the number of suites in the hotel, said this met the local requirements of the village of Long Branch and also of the township of Etobicoke. Now, I have another quotation from Mr. McCallum addressing the Long Branch council-
Would the hon. member mind a question because I am following this with great interest? Who is this bird, Mr. McCallum?

Well, sir, I don't know. Lawyers are a dime a dozen in Toronto. I have never met this gentleman. His name is here-James McCallum. It does not say anything about his firm. I guess he is on his own. It says he is spokesman for Millgate Park Investments Ltd. Now, here is an interesting quotation. Mr. McCallum said:
The question of whether the fill is there or not is not of the greatest concern.
Well, the Minister of Justice backs him up in that.
Now, I wish to point this out in connection with the illegal fill, and I use this word because I borrow it from Martha Brewin of the N.D.P. This is quoting Reeve Tom Berry who wants assessment increases, and he says:
The fill is in the lake now, and won't be taken out. Don't underestimate the power of the developers.
What I have to say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to Mr. Berry is this-I have unfortunately overestimated the power of the cabinet, the power of the Minister of Transport and the power of the Minister of Public Works. I suppose Mr. Berry was watching the provinces pushing the federal government around and he felt the municipalities should get into the act too.
I have already mentioned that Mr. Berry has been quoted as saying that legality is of secondary importance to Long Branch, that they want increased assessment. There are many of us here who have sat under lawyers, men versed in the law, who have stood up and told us we are living in the age of law and if we all observed the law everything would be perfect. Judges and lawyers state that law is the basis of our civilization. -next to sewers. But here we have Reeve Berry pointing out that legality is of secondary importance and assessment comes first, and he is ably aided and abetted by Crawford Bell, Chairman of the Long Branch
Supply-Transport
Planning Board who, at the meeting Mr. McCallum was at, said:
Legality is of interest, but has no direct connection with us.
I come to the conclusion that the cabinet must be coming to the same opinion as the Chairman of the Long Branch Planning Board. Long Branch, after all, must have a population of about 1,200 souls and, when they want to increase assessment, who is to stop them heaving fill into the lake and trying to have it zoned by the proper people as fit to hold two 18 storey towers housing over 200 suites each?
I have here a letter dated January 21, 1965, which tells Millgate Park Investments that they have to stop the filling. This is written by the engineer in Toronto, and I refer to it again because of the paragraph which states:
I was further informed that as at December 1st, 1964, the fill extended 470 feet into Lake Ontario with an average width of 330 feet.
If you multiply that out you will find it comes to 3J acres in land surface. This land is right inside the boundaries of metropolitan Toronto and is valued at anywhere from $100,000 to $200,000 an acre. You could imagine what kind of money would be advanced under the National Housing Act to the owner of 3i acres of land in Lake Ontario unless some objection is taken to his title, and am objecting on behalf of some thousands of people who live along that lake shore.
There is an application before the Department of Public Works which will definitely interfere with navigation, a matter which comes under the Department of Transport. This application is for a permit to erect a cribwork around this 400 foot peninsula, but the cribwork application states it is to extend for 660 feet, 220 feet further out into the lake. The cribwork will require piles 16 feet in length. Water that requires 16 foot piles won't take the Queen Mary, the Queen Elizabeth or some of the new Japanese oil tankers, but around Lake Ontario many boats come closer to the shore than 440 feet. Their draught is not as great as 16 foot piles would require, and these will interfere seriously with navigation.
In this letter from the engineer, dated January 21, 1965, he writes:
It has been brought to my attention recently that not only has this fill been placed without prior approval of the Department of Public Works, pursuant to the Navigable Waters Protection Act, but that in addition thereto the fill was left unprotected and consequently caused erosion under the wave action of the lake. I further understand


Supply-Transport
that the eroded material has been deposited along the shore to such an extent that a storm sewer outfall adjacent to the fill is now 150 feet from the shoreline, a true indication that the material is being deposited in navigable waters with a possible detrimental effect on navigation.
Then he goes on to say:
On the assumption that you should immediately comply with the above instruction and requirements-
Note, it is only an assumption on the government's part. It does not expect this person to follow the law.
On the assumption that you should immediately comply with the above instructions and requirements, you are requested pursuant to section 5(2) (b) of the said act for the purpose of rendering the total existing fill lawful, to apply for approval of the said existing fill five years after its completion.
This means they should stop the filling, but will have more and more erosion for five years, and then five years afterwards they may apply for permission to erect cribwork. But the letter added:
This would mean that you should not place any additional fill at this location.
Should you fail to adhere to my instructions, consideration will be given for the complete removal of the fill, at your expense, pursuant to section 5 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
This is the letter that the same Mr. McCallum told the Long Branch Council that they had lost and that it did not turn up until March 4. He told them that they found the letter on March 4, six weeks later.
Is this Mr. McCallum the counsel for this firm?

I am not a lawyer. I presume if he is the legal adviser, as these newspapers say, then presumably he is the counsel for them too. However, this is the letter which they said they lost, but of course between January 21 and March 4 they put in a lot more fill. Then they stopped it, and there has not been any more fill put in for the past
year__a year come March. However, erosion
has continued and the property owners right and left of this project are complaining bitterly about the treatment they are getting from the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Justice when they ask that the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act and the Navigable Waters Protection Act be
enforced.	.
I prefer to take the opinion expressed m the department of works letter of January that this is an obstacle to navigation, rather than the statement of the Minister of Justice that it is not.

I have a picture here of some of the fill. It projects 30 feet into the air out from the shore. I had men stand beside it so that one can get a comparison of its height. This fill would stop the Royal Navy's biggest battleship if it ever got into Lake Ontario, yet we are told it is not an obstacle.
My hon. friend, the member for Russell, said to me when he saw this, "I don't know why you complain about these things. I really don't. They are building a sand beach. Those thousands of cinderblocks sticking out in the lake are where little children are going to warm their tootsies."	_
These were being dumped in the fill until we got it stopped by protesting, but now they want to build a crib around it.
Table the photograph.

I would be very happy to do so.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I would ask the government to enforce the Navigable Waters Protection Act and to observe the terms of the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act, first and foremost for the health of the people; second, to look after the navigable needs of the people living on the shores of lake Ontario and, third, to look after the interest of the power companies. I would ask the minister to tell the power interests that the lake Ontario water level must always be maintained at a minimum of 244.78 feet, which has been the average for the past 94 years.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman a question? In British Columbia the law does not permit this sort of thing without the consent of the riparian owners. Were the individuals who are the property owners along the lakeshore consulted and did they give their consent to this construction?

Mr. Chairman, I asked the question a year ago, when pointing out this situation, whether consent had been given by the International Joint Commission or the Department of Public Works in respect of any fill between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek. In fact, I asked my original question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on March 25 last, and I have not yet received a reply. However, the hon. member for Northumberland, who was then a parliamentary secretary, said that no permits had been issued for fill at any time between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek, a


distance of four miles in which there are 20 or 30 pieces of property that have been filled.
The private owners of property along the lakeshore were not consulted, is that right?

These people who own the waterlots-the private owners-have filled in their own waterlots in many areas between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek and have apparently set a precedent for the rest of the owners and for the rest of time.
Mr. Chairman, I have asked the government continually to get a ruling from the Supreme Court of Canada as to what are the legal rights of the owners of waterlots. The Minister of Public Works stood up recently and said that he was not clear himself in this regard, and expressed the wish that somebody would clear this up for him. I have asked the government to refer this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada, but no action has been taken. The Minister of Justice suggested that my request was vague. Let me spell it out for him. I should like to have the cabinet make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada, asking for a decision as to what are the legal rights of the owners of patented waterlots on the shores of Lake Ontario. If that is vague I shall have to learn French, because that is as plain as I can put it in English.

Mr. Chairman, the evening is growing late and the minister has had a long day so I will just make a few brief remarks in the time that remains. I shall journey on this travelogue of the Department of Transport from the sewers in Montreal to clear waters on the east coast.
I was particularly interested in the speech made by the hon. member for Kindersley. It was an excellent speech in which he put forward the suggestions and submissions of importance to his province and to the western part of Canada. I was particularly interested in the matter of railway abandonments. That hon. member of course also mentioned the matter of box cars. Let me state that these box cars are constructed in a plant in the area of my constituency. I can assure the minister that we are ready for more orders at any time and he can advise the Canadian National Railways to that effect. Very often, when he originally took that portfolio, I bothered him about this subject. This plant has been changed and diversified and it can now handle a great many more orders.
Supply-Transport
The hon. member for Kindersley mentioned the proposed bill which will come before the house, and perhaps before the Committee on Transportation. My name is listed among the members of that committee and I look forward to a great deal of interesting work in that regard during this session.
The hon. member for Kindersley also mentioned that he believed, in respect of the matter of abandonments-there are perhaps two in my constituency-that the figures presented by the Canadian National Railways should not be accepted alone and by themselves. If there is to be a rationalization agency, or some type of agency set up under the proposed legislation by the Minister of Transport, I hope there will be some means and some mechanics of making other figures available, as well as the figures presented by the C.N.R.
There are two proposed abandonments in my area, one which runs from Vernal to Sunnybrae, to the end of the steel, which is the old line built by the old Nova Scotia Railway Company and taken over by the Colonial. I think the hon. member for Antig-onish-Guysborough will back me up when I state that this was the start of the Guys-borough Railway Company.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: When is that to be reactivated?

I will have to ask the
Minister of Transport, but if you will back me up in that regard, perhaps we will ask for that as well.
The other proposed abandonment is in respect of a piece of junk, I call it-to be blunt, the guts of the short line which is a piece of line from Tatamagouche to Scotsburn, a distance of 24 miles. The proposal of the Canadian National Railways is to take the junk out of the middle and let us run cars at both ends. We know what will happen then. Of course, that will sound the death knell to this short piece of line.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to thank the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) for having so obligingly accepted to prolong his stay in the house in order to answer the question I wish to put to him.
The competence of the minister impresses us all to such an extent that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself wished to proclaim it.
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister could, this evening, throw some light on a topic I consider of prime importance. Last year the government published a white paper on capital punishment.
The session was cut short and the election followed. The Speech from the Throne read last January 18 states:
Arrangements will be made for you to decide the issue of capital punishment at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that the the prospective debate on capital punishment should be delayed as much as possible because I think the time is not ripe for such a debate, for the following reasons:
February 10. 1966	COMMONS
In the first place, criminality is rising frightfully and there is a terrific number of murders being committed. I will have the opportunity of giving to the house a few statistics concerning the province of Quebec.
I shall take a given period, that is from 1955 to 1960. During that period, an average of 41 murders were committed each year in the province of Quebec only, which is 12 per cent more than in the previous five-year period, or from 1951 to 1955 inclusive.
From 1961 to 1965, there was, in the province of Quebec, an average of 57 murders per year, that is 28 per cent more during the period when the new government mitigated the penalty by commuting the death sentence.
Therefore, I suggest, first, that it is not the appropriate time to hold such a debate, because of a frightening outbreak of crime and, second, because public feeling in favour of a solution, either for its complete abolition, its maintenance, or its modified abolition, is still not clear.
I hardly think this is an opportune time to discuss the death penalty since the government has created a commission of inquiry. I must congratulate the minister for tabling the report of the committee on juvenile deliquen-cy, a most impressive report, exceptionally informative.
Last year the government set up a committee called the Canadian Committee on Penal and Correctional Reform. The terms of reference of this committee are to study the extent of crime in this country. The committee is to report on the causes of crime. I would not say the committee intends to be restricted to these matters only, but it is surely one of its basic responsibilities to report.
I am surprised at that eagerness for the abolition of capital punishment, when that committee has not yet filed its report. I am not blaming the committee, because it has just been established.
I would ask the minister whether he would not deem it expedient to suggest that the said committee table its report. If that report cannot be tabled in the near future, may I

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), who addressed the house with his usual ease and in a masterly fashion, for his personal and very generous remarks toward the Solicitor General. I wish also to make it meticulously plain that on the issue of capital punishment I speak only for myself and not in the character as Solicitor General. I believe that capital punishment is not a matter for party formula. I believe every member in the house will approach it as a matter of conscience and intellectual conviction.
May I say to the hon. member, without offence, that I do not think his speech sufficiently reflected the work that I am sure he knows has gone into the White Paper on capital punishment. It is an admirable approach, a dispassionate and objective approach to a very difficult problem. So far as the matter of an interim report from the Committee on Corrections is concerned, I wish to point out that this committee has barely begun to enter upon its deliberations. This is a committee chaired by Mr. Justice Ouimet and has an outstanding committee membership. It would, in the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, be manifestly unfair and unrealistic to expect this committee to bring forth an interim report on such a formidable subject when, and I hope I am not going too far, the house expects an early debate on this subject.
In conclusion may I express the personal desire that penal reform in this country in the next few years will indicate that the mind and spirit of man has kept pace with our material and scientific advances.

CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING UNIVERSITY GRANTS Copy of letter sent to all provincial premiers except Quebec.
Ottawa, January 17, 1966.
The Honourable W. Ross Thatcher, M.L.A.,
Premier of Saskatchewan,
Regina, Saskatchewan.
My dear Premier:
The Government of Canada and the Governments of the Provinces received last October proposals submitted jointly to them by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. The Association strongly endorsed the general recommendations contained in the Report of the Commission on the Financing of Higher Education in Canada and urged earnest consideration of them by the federal and provincial governments.
In my statement to the press on October 14, 1965, on the subject of the financing of higher education, I welcomed the submission by the Association and accepted on behalf of the federal government a responsibility to consider these recommendations which had been directed to the federal government as well as to the provincial governments. I emphasized, however, that the response to these important recommendations on the financing of higher education in Canada should be a joint response of the provincial and federal governments, and undertook to propose to the provinces a special federal-provincial conference to consider the universities' proposals.
Circumstances have not permitted an early federal-provincial conference for this purpose and at the meeting in December of the Tax Structure Committee, it was suggested that the federal government should make a decision concerning interim arrangements for the academic year 1966-67 without waiting for a general conference, bearing in mind that it is normal for the provincial governments to review university budgets in the month of January. Having this in mind and also that the provincial governments will wish to incorporate in their own budgets a level of support appropriate to the needs of the universities in 1966-67, the federal government has decided to adopt this suggested interim procedure. I am writing now to outline the proposals which the federal government plans to submit to Parliament in respect of the academic year 1966-67. In order to
consider the longer term responses of the federal and provincial governments and the relationship between them, it will be necessary to discuss them at a federal-provincial conference, perhaps the one we have planned for Victoria, and I will be writing to you about this at a later date.
The arrangement outlined below will be applicable to the academic year 1966-67 only and is made without prejudice to that which may obtain thereafter. This interim arrangement deals only with an increase in grants which should help materially to meet the operating costs of the universities. The federal government does not feel that it can respond to the recommendations of the universities concerning grants for capital expenditures before they have been discussed carefully with the provincial governments.
The federal government is prepared for the academic year 1966-67 to increase its per capita operating grants to $5.00 per capita of the population of Canada. In those provinces other than Quebec, the grants would be paid as now to the universities that are recognized as being eligible for such grants by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. For Quebec, the arrangement at present existing will be continued and, to give effect to the increase in the per capita grants, a cash payment would be made to bring total federal assistance to that province to a level which is in proportion by population to what all other provinces are receiving. The fact that the organization and institutions of education in Quebec are considerably different from those in other provinces warrants, in our view, the continuation of special arrangements with Quebec in respect of these grants.
In considering the form of payments through the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the federal government feels that something additional should be included in the grants to universities in those provinces that take a higher proportion of out-of-province students. To give effect to this principle the grants will be paid in the form of a basic grant of approximately $4.30 per capita of the population of each of the provinces concerned, supplemented by an

amount per out-of-province student in each province equal to the average of the basic grant per student in all these provinces. These basic grants together with the supplementary grants will provide an average of $5.00 per capita, but the distribution to universities will be higher in those provinces with a higher ratio of out-of-province students. In the final application of this formula, provincial populations on June 1, 1966 and the total students and out-of-province students enrolled in eligible universities in each province in the academic year 1966-67 will be based on up to date estimates by the Dominion Statistician. In the meantime, tentative estimates have been made and it is suggested that you use for planning purposes the following amounts as indicating the probable orders of magnitude of total grants:
Newfoundland, $2,250,000; Prince Edward Island $615,000; Nova Scotia, $5,055,000; New Brunswick, $5,040,000; Ontario, $33,370,000; Manitoba, $5,090,000; Saskatchewan, $4,485,000; Alberta, $7,050,000; British Columbia, $8,890,000.
An interim payment will be made in September, based on the then available estimates of provincial populations. A second instalment will be paid in January, after the enrollment of total students and out-of-province students is known. The final instalment would be paid early in May. The distribution of the grants to eligible institutions within each province will be in accordance with the formula proposed in the submission by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada.
It is my earnest hope that the above interim arrangement for federal operating grants to universities, together with the action which your government and other provincial governments will take in respect of the needs of universities in the academic year 1966-67, will constitute a constructive step forward in making a joint response to the need for adequate financing of higher education in Canada. It would, of course, leave to the provinces full responsibility for legislation in respect of university affairs.
I shall be sending a letter tomorrow to the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada informing them of this plan. They should be of assistance to provincial authorities in working out how it may be expected to apply to individual institutions on the new weighting formula which they have proposed and we have accepted.
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson.

Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I was very pleased to receive your letter of January 17, regarding larger federal grants for higher education.
It is not the wish of the Government of British Columbia to control the federal university grants in any way, yet I am concerned as to the division among the different universities. We have in our Province three public universities and one private university, and our Government is in favour of the policy that now exists that all four universities receive benefits from the federal grants for higher education.
In regard to the three public universities, I believe it would be good policy if the federal grants and the provincial grants are dovetailed in a way so that our three public universities would feel that they would receive equal treatment.
In the Province of British Columbia, as Minister of Finance, I do not set the individual operating grants for each public university, but set the money up in a total amount in a block vote, and then a permanent finance committee, which is set up by the three universities themselves, arrange for the division of these monies after a full study of their respective budgets, and I would hope that you would agree, Mr. Prime Minister, that the share of federal grants that will be going to our public universities would be divided by the same university committee.
With kindest personal regards, I remain,
Yours very truly,
